#7490. The midterms and SCOTUS

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In the aftermath of Election Day, Republicans and Democrats alike are grappling with what the blue wave means for the Supreme Court. Keep reading to learn how the Senate shake-up, in particular, could affect when a justice next leaves the court and how the confirmation process might unfold.

Plus, one year ago today, the justices heard argument in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, a challenge to President Donald Trump’s tariff regime. Just over three months later, the Supreme Court struck down the tariffs, holding that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not give the president the authority to impose tariffs.

On Wednesday, the justices heard argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, on the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review.

Tomorrow, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from Friday’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the justices to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request is now fully briefed, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

Recommended Citation: Kelsey Dallas, The midterms and SCOTUS, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 5, 2026, 9:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-midterms-and-scotus/

We're looking for our first Product Operations Manager. Our product team is small, senior, and growing fast, with each PM coming in to establish the foundations of a new part of the business. As the team grows, the work that connects it (how we plan, set and measure goals, keep the roadmap honest, run our rituals, learn from customers, and bring new people up to speed) needs an owner.

This role is that owner. Your customers are the PMs and the head of product, and your job is to make them faster and better at what they do. You won't be inheriting a process manual or enforcing one. You'll be designing how a product team works at the moment it goes from a handful of people to a real organization, inside an engineering culture that values autonomy and only adopts what makes people's lives easier.

see the people you support as customers, and start from their problems rather than from a framework

like building systems from scratch more than maintaining them

would rather remove a meeting than add one

write clearly and enjoy making complicated things legible

are a fast learner, frequently picking up new tools and techniques, including AI

The best way to impress us is by trying LiveKit's product, understanding how we work, and bringing smart thoughts and opinions to the table.

Run the product team's operating cadence. You own the calendar of planning cycles, reviews, and recurring updates: what each one is for, who needs to be there, what goes in, and what comes out. You make sure decisions and follow-ups are captured and visible to everyone who needs them, and you keep retiring or reshaping rituals that stop earning their time.

Own the roadmap as a system. You own how the roadmap is structured, at the right altitude for each audience, from engineering teams to leadership to sales. You make sure it stays current and becomes the place people go to find out what we're building and where it stands.

Make goals and progress visible. You run goal-setting for the product team so that every goal is measurable against a clear source of truth, and you track progress against those goals through the quarter. With our data team, you own the reporting the product team and leadership rely on, and you flag drift early.

Keep the product development playbook. You maintain lightweight shared standards for each step from framing a problem through launch: problem briefs, launch readiness, product stage definitions, release notes. With marketing, you run the internal side of every launch so each one ships with docs, pricing, and GTM ready.

Run the customer insight engine. You own the systems that keep customers close to the product team: a research repository people use, a continuous pipeline of customer conversations set up with sales and success, and a steady synthesis of what we hear from sales, support, surveys, and deals, delivered to the PMs who need it.

Grow the craft of the PM team. You own onboarding for new PMs, ongoing training, and the team's community of practice, and you help shape how we hire and level PMs.

Choose and run the team's tools. You decide how the product team uses its tools, from roadmapping and analytics to AI, and you make sure PMs get real leverage from them.

Be a partner in running the product org. You keep a pulse on where the team is stuck, bring your own point of view on what to fix next, and work with the head of product to make the product org better every quarter.

6+ years of experience, with at least 3 in product operations or a closely related role (chief of staff to a product leader, product program management, product strategy and operations) supporting a product team.

You've built it before. You've designed a product team's operating cadence from scratch at a company that was scaling, not only kept an existing one running.

A force multiplier. You measure your success by what changed for the people you support, not by how much process exists.

Data fluent. You're comfortable defining metrics, working in BI tools, and telling a trustworthy number from an untrustworthy one. SQL is a plus.

#7471. Senior Legal Counsel, Product & Privacy at Kit

Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

You'll report to our Chief Operating Officer, Brian Bevel, and partner regularly with leaders across product, sales, finance, and people operations. You'll own our core legal work in-house, reduce the need for outside counsel, and know when specialized outside counsel is truly needed.

Deep expertise in data, compliance, and product—this is where you'll spend most of your time.

Experience supporting customer security questionnaires and partnering effectively with security, sales, product, and engineering teams

Understanding of intellectual property law, especially related to brand, content, and software

Understanding of commercial contracts—you'll become the go-to person for these at Kit.

Clear communicator and trusted advisor—able to simplify complexity and help others make informed decisions

Experience as in-house counsel at a tech company or serving a tech portfolio at a top-tier firm that's well-known for their work with startups (e.g., Fenwick & West, Cooley)

J.D. from an accredited law school in the United States

Active member in good standing of a State Bar Association

Strategic thinker who sees legal as a lever, not a blocker

Deeply curious and business-oriented—you start by understanding the goals, then explore the smartest paths to get there.

Collaborative partner who can navigate conflict productively

Deep belief that creator success is our success—you consider both Kit and our customers in every recommendation

A "how might we" problem-solver who finds creative, business-aligned paths through legal challenges

Needing a team of in-house peers or co-counsel to pressure-test every decision—you'll be our sole in-house legal expert, with outside counsel available as needed

A strongly risk-averse or "no-before-yes" mindset—we need you to help us move, not just stop us from tripping

Thinking in a legal vacuum—if you're not factoring in our goals, numbers, or creators, your advice won't land

Struggling with speed or ownership—if you prefer long timelines or wait to be told what to do, this won't be the right environment. We move quickly and expect people to take initiative, spot problems, and drive solutions.

We're 100% remote with team members across the globe. For this role, we're looking for someone located in the United States.

Kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. This role is an individual contributor level 4 ($227,000) or 5 ($252,000). Our other perks and benefits include:

We cover up to $2,100 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance plans through Aetna

$2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Company-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget

Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year)

Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON

Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment

Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work

Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days

Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year

Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months

Winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period

Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team

Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year

We usually receive a large number of applications, and our goal is to follow up with you within two weeks. You’ll hear from us either way. Here’s what you can expect from the rest of our hiring process:

A phone screen with our recruiter (30 min)

Panel interview with cross functional stakeholders (60 min)

We’ll keep you informed through every step. To get started, complete this application, including a cover letter and answers to the questions on the next page. We read every single application, and your cover letter and responses help put your experience into context.

We value diversity in all of its forms. Research tells us that applicants who are female or non-binary, as well as applicants who are people of color, are less likely to apply for roles they do not feel 100% qualified for. If you think you meet more than 50% of our requirements but fewer than 100% of them, please apply.

We’re imperfect communicators, so think of our job postings as the starting point for discussion rather than proof that you shouldn’t apply.

#7444. YouTube is giving some creators a 30-day fix-it period before terminating their channels

YouTube is giving some creators a little grace after flagging their channels for violations of its spam policy.

The new path YouTube is testing will give them a chance to fix the (alleged) errors of their ways and get their channels back up.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Under the new process, once a channel is flagged, it will be removed from public viewership–but will not be deleted.

Instead, “it will enter a 30-day locked period and the channel owner will be notified via email and in YouTube Studio on desktop,” Team YouTube wrote in a Help Center post. “Certain actions, such as uploading new videos or posting comments, will not be available while your channel is locked.”

During the 30-day lock, creators have three options:

Here’s the section of the policy that has us wondering: “Automated or synthetic mass-production: Using automated tools or AI to churn out high volumes of similar content with minimal changes. While testing out new creation tools or posting a few variations of a video is ok, we don’t allow use of these tools to flood our platform with repetitive content. This includes coordinated mass-production and technical manipulation to bypass filters or trick viewers.”

Examples of violators include channels that “use the exact same background music and repetitive AI generated imagery across many videos, with each video reading out an AI-generated script.”

This policy sounds good, but YouTube’s attempts to curb AI slop (even as Google dumps enough money into the AI bubble to keep itself in the red for the last two quarters) have backlashed onto genuine creators.

A number of creators–like stop-motion channel Tiny Grandma–have had their content incorrectly flagged as AI and demonetized. The folks behind Tiny Grandma reached out to us here at Tubefilter when YouTube stripped their monetization, and we were able to connect them directly with humans at YouTube. But what about creators who can’t get the hookup, and instead are stuck with automated responses?

This new process might help address that concern–but that’s if the process becomes widely used.

Team YouTube does mention that the 30-day grace period is an experiment, and that only certain channels are eligible. We don’t know what the eligibility requirements are–and, as always with YouTube experiments, it’s possible this one won’t ever make it to live service for all users. Seems like it would be nice if it did, though.

For now, the Video Kickstart Bonus is a pilot program that is being tested among a select group of creators. Those lab rats will be notified of their eligibility via their Creator Studio dashboards. Once they join the program, they must post 15 “qualifying videos” on 15 different days across a predetermined “period.” X’s Video Kickstart Bonus rules do not specify exactly how long each period is.

Upon completion of that task, participating creators will be rewarded with bonuses that could be up to $3,000 in value. U.S.-based creators will be paid through the X Money account while creators in other territories will be able to cash out through a connected Stripe account.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

If this setup sounds familiar, it’s because YouTube just announced something similar a few days ago. The YouTube Shorts Bonus Program is a revenue stream that rewards consistency, and like X’s Video Kickstart Bonus, the YouTube program is currently being tested on an invite-only basis.

In our coverage of the YouTube Shorts Bonus Program, we noted that the platform could be promoting consistency to build a bigger library of original content. That seems to be X’s goal as well. Like Instagram, X is allocating payouts to those who post original videos. The test subjects for the Video Kickstart Bonus will be fast-tracked into the Original Content Rewards Program, which X launched earlier this year.

For X, the development of more reliable revenue streams has been a years-long process. Now, that monetization is arriving in multiple forms, and in return, X will get the robust videomaking community it has long coveted.

#7437. YouTube enlists educational creators to show the value of its interactive gaming hub

As educators, researchers, and policymakers debate YouTube’s utility in classrooms, a handful of creators are getting the chance to show how the platform’s interactive elements can enhance learning. YouTube quietly introduced a slate of educational games through its Playables hub, with notable STEM channels like Veritasium and Khan Academy involved in the initiative.

Playables has been available on YouTube for nearly three years, but for much of its existence, the hub has been little more than a motley collection of low-stakes, casual titles. Though YouTube has tested some upgrades for its gaming destination, the reach and influence of Playables pale in comparison to YouTube’s traditional video library.

Last week, YouTube showed that Playables could have significant potential in scholastic settings. With its six-game library of educational titles, YouTube is helping players learn about subjects like physics, economics, and music theory within fun, interactive settings.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Veritasium’s contribution to the new gaming library is Elements of Truth, a simple trivia challenge that tests players’ scientific knowledge. According to Luke Lewis, the Director of Publishing at Electrify Video Partners — which invested in Veritasium in 2023 — YouTube came calling earlier this year to propose Playables tie-ins for Electrify’s brands. Lewis told Tubefilter that Electrify saw the proposal as an opportunity to promote Veritasium’s Elements of Truth tabletop game.

“Our long-term expectations are for the game to introduce Elements of Truth to an audience of knowledge-hungry casual gamers who might otherwise not be familiar with it – and in fact might not even be familiar with Veritasium‘s videos,” Lewis said. “At the same time, we hope it will deepen engagement among existing Veritasium fans, encourage them to get competitive with fellow fans, and have fun doing it.”

Lewis said that the initial response to the Playables title has been “extremely positive.” Orders for the physical Elements of Truth game have spiked as Veritasium fans have shared their Playables high scores with each other.

As useful as Playables has been for Electrify and Veritasium, it might be even more valuable for YouTube itself. Though the platform has thrown resources behind educational initiatives led by top creators, it has also faced ban threats in schools, most notably in the New York City school district. Detractors may argue that a platform like YouTube can only be a distraction in the classroom, but games like Elements of Truth suggest otherwise.

In previous years, interactive games on YouTube have been the domain of marketing agencies and tech-savvy tinkerers. Perhaps, given the positive response Electrify has seen, we’re about to enter into an era of good-for-you games on Google’s video platform. YouTube is certainly committed to promoting Playables. It recently introduced accessability tags that help users find the games that best fit their device’s settings. So if you want to try to beat my Elements of Truth high score (which won’t be too hard), finding and playing the game should be a cinch.

#7434. Top 5 Branded Videos of the Week: The adrenaline spectrum

Welcome to our rundown of the most-watched branded YouTube videos of the week.

We’re publishing this snippet of a larger Gospel Stats Weekly Brand Report in order to analyze sponsorship trends in the creator economy. Any video launched in tandem with an official brand partner is eligible for t he ranking.

And–as the name up above would imply–all the data comes from Gospel Stats. If you’re interested in learning more about Gospel–and which brands are sponsoring what creators on YouTube–click here. You can also download our YouTube 2025 Sponsorship Landscape Report here.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

This week’s Gospel Stats Brand Report kicks off with an adrenaline rush and then tapers into a nice relaxing day trip to the lake. In between, we’ve got a YouTube-sponsored video, some questionable fitness decisions, and more.

#1 If You Escape, You Win $1,000,000 Channel: MrBeast Gaming and Call of Duty Brand: Call of Duty Views: 56,792,187

Something something we got MrBeast in Call of Duty before GTA 6.

There’s $1 million on the line in Jimmy Beast’s new collab with CoD promotes its latest Modern Warfare installment–and specifically the game’s “DMZ” mode, which pits players against each other and the environment around them. With NPC dangers lurking, players can choose to team up for safety in numbers…but eventually all bonds must break, as only one team can emerge victorious.

MrBeast’s video drops 10 teams into a real-life army camp where they split into their own technologically tricked out tents and hop into a DMZ match. The last team alive in-game keeps the cash prize IRL.

MrBeast called this collab a “dream come true,” and we’re guessing CoD‘s developers might feel similarly, considering the view count for this video. They also produced a Short together this week; that one came in at #9 on our list, with more than 12 million views.

#2 I cant stop listening to the song ? @YouTube #YouTubePartner #sofimanassyan #LISA Channel: Sofi Manassyan Brand: YouTube Views: 26,314,085

Blackpink‘s YouTube dominance might never fade. Its frontwoman dancer and rapper, LISA, is square in the spotlight for this new YouTube-sponsored promo.

Manyassan doesn’t mention her sponsor till the last couple seconds of the video, where, through faux fan tears, she tells viewers to go watch more LISA content on YouTube.

This is an intriguing one for us. YouTube has historically rarely sponsored creators–but in the past couple years, it’s brought groups of creators to major events like the World Cup, teamed up with Mark Rober for his STEM education initiative, and signed a multiyear partnership with MrBeast that spans numerous Google products. (There’s also the thing with it paying creators to stay off Netflix.)

And, on top of its creator team-ups, YouTube has been pushing its Music service, one of the key areas where it competes with other platforms like Spotify. Combining the two might be some pretty strong sauce.

#3 I Survived Chinas Fat Loss Prison Channel: Browney Brand: Gymshark, Myprotein Views: 18,223,893

MrBeast isn’t the only channel hitting our top 5 with a weight loss challenge video. The difference is, Browney himself is the one in the hot seat.

He went to China and sent himself to one of the country’s “fat loss prisons,” where people who want to lose weight voluntarily (at least, it’s supposed to be voluntary) enter and are not allowed to leave until they’ve gotten skinnier. While they’re in the “prison,” people sleep in dorms, do four hours of exercise a day, and have strictly controlled meals.

Browney, whose YouTube tagline is “everything is a challenge,” spends 50 hours in the place getting to know his fellow “inmates,” hearing their stories, and experiencing what they’re going through to lose weight. Perhaps unsurprisingly, his upload is sponsored by two fitness brands: workout clothing company Gymshark and supplement company Myprotein.

#4 Riding 1300 Miles to Alaska on Jet Ski – Camping & Fishing Channel: Matt Spears Brand: AnyDesk Views: 17,221,584

This two-hour odyssey of a video chronicles creator Matt Spears‘ much longer odyssey. He recently became the first person to jetski up the West Coast of the U.S., along the shores of Canada, and up to Alaska. It was an enormous undertaking: 1,300 miles of near-constant travel, all his gear and fuel packed into one vehicle, and nobody to rely on but himself.

His accomplishment has racked up more than 17 million views for his sponsor AnyDesk, and is part of the company’s overall creator support initiative.

“If you have any ridiculous experiments that you would love to see your favorite YouTubers test online you can submit them here. If you submit an idea that ends up being used for a video we will ship you some swag and potentially a prop from one of the videos,” AnyDesk–which makes remote desktop software–said on a landing page linked by Spears. “At AnyDesk, we’re passionate about science, creativity, and collaboration. Whether it’s testing a car battery-powered computer or building something completely ridiculous, we love connecting people who think outside the box.”

AnyDesk also sponsored two other videos this week: #537 from Scammer Payback, and #944 from Trilogy Media.

BONUS #5,029 autumn in los angeles | unique coffee recipes, lake arrowhead day trip Channel: Brandon Chou Brand: Away Views: 43,527

So much of our YouTube feeds these days are ultra-high-energy shoutfests, super-tuned to keep viewers glued as long as possible. It can feel like a treat when something comes up and no one’s yelling at you or going Taken with the editing.

Slow and easy is the vibe with Brandon Chou‘s week-in-the-life vlog, where he leaves L.A. behind and takes viewers up to Lake Arrowhead, which is nestled in the San Bernardino National Forest at 5,000 feet elevation. Being that close to the sky means lots of great shots, and Chou lingers on them as he and his friends walk through the local shops, pick up ingredients to make dinner in their Airbnb, and roast marshmallows to the sound of lapping water.

The video is, fittingly, sponsored by luggage company Away, and though Chou’s plug for the company is relatively short, his entire vlog lures viewers with a call-to-action, telling them: get out of the city, away from the stress, and go look at something beautiful.

…and there’s a lot more data where that came from. If you like our Weekly Top 5, you’ll love everything else Gospel has to offer.

#7431. The code for YouTube’s Android app reveals a testing ground for Instagram-style social features

The most recent version of YouTube‘s Android app includes some curious lines of code. A report from Android Authority reveals numerous references to Tamba, a mysterious entity that has some similarities to Instagram.

Android Authority‘s discoveries within the YouTube app include the logo pictured above and dozens of icons that share a crude aesthetic reminiscent of hand-drawn images. Those assets are tied to a package titled “com.google.android.youtube.sandbox,” suggesting that Tamba is a separate experience from the primary version of YouTube.

Based on the use of the word “sandbox” in that string, one hypothesis is that Tamba is nothing more than an experimental platform used to test new features before they’re pushed to YouTube. But Android Authority notes that the code references a separate “test” package, which means that Tamba could be something more than a digital lab.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Some of the terms used in the Tamba assets sound more like what you’d expect to see on Instagram rather than YouTube. There are references to followers, direct messages, and group chats. Tamba’s chats may also be able to integrate formats from the main version of YouTube, including Shorts.

If YouTube is trying to develop its own take on Instagram, it wouldn’t be the first tech company to utilize that strategy. Meta’s perceived abandonment of the qualities that made O.G. Instagram so popular have opened up opportunities for rivals. The photo app Dispo, for example, enjoyed a brief surge by telling its users that it’s not Instagram. More recently, TikTok embraced different types of photo content as part of an effort to revive the bygone Instagram experience.

YouTube, for its part, has built up its DMs as Instagram has turned those messages into a revenue stream. DMs haven’t traditionally been a big part of YouTube’s approach to community, but if Tamba is a real thing, it could put that form of correspondance front and center.

Of course, that’s a big if. YouTube runs all sorts of tests all the time, and it’s important to accept that Tamba could ultimately amount to little. But Instagram is eager to encroach on YouTube’s territory by allowing long-form video uploads. It wouldn’t be a surprise if YouTube returned the favor.

#7426. Midterm election traffic spiked on Twitch, but Hasan Piker can’t hold a candle to Steve Kornacki

The 2026 U.S. midterm elections resulted in a historic victory for Democrats, but liberals weren’t the only big winners on the night of November 3. Streamers across YouTube, Twitch, Kick, and Rumble picked up more viewership than they’ve ever received during midterm election coverage.

According to Streams Charts, election-related broadcasts on those four platforms combined to haul in 20.87 hours of watch time, collectively reaching 3.4 million concurrent viewers. Across 3,400 channels, election night traffic was more than four times higher than it was during the previous midterms in 2022. (Streams during the presidential election year of 2024, however, did deliver more traffic.)

The increasing midterms viewership on streaming platforms underscored creators’ growing influence in American politics. After Trump used his connections with creators to gain ground in 2024, Democrats fought back by forging their own alliances. Several of the biggest winners in 2026 — including Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, and Texas Senator-elect James Talarico — boosted their campaigns through robust social media strategies.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

The results of that push can be seen on Streams Charts‘ list of the most-watched midterms broadcasts of 2026. Progressive lightning rod Hasan Piker attracted 1.75 million hours of watch time on his November 3 Twitch stream. On the right side of the aisle, Steven Crowder made a big impression on Rumble, bringing in 461,000 hours of watch time.

One of the U.S. Congressional reps who has recognized the political power of creators is California Democrat Ro Khanna. As the so-called blue tsunami crashed down, Khanna stopped by Piker’s Twitch stream and said that his colleagues shouldn’t fear Piker’s influence.

“You would think, after this showing around the country, more people would say ‘yeah, you know what, we may not agree with him on everything, but he’s got a huge following,'” Khanna said. “People across the country are resonating with things that he’s saying about the war. Yeah, maybe we should engage.”

Piker does have a huge following, but even the archetypical himbo can’t keep up with a dorky data analyst who loves rolled-up sleeves and bellwether counties. NBC News went all-in on Steve Kornacki and his “Kornacki Cam” during the midterms, and that turned out to be the right move. Kornacki’s breakdown of the blue tsunami collected 29 million views across all platforms to become the #1 election stream. Per Streams Charts, NBC News picked up 4.39 million hours of election night watch time on YouTube.

So while the size of the blue tsunami may have eclipsed predictions, the distribution of electoral coverage was exactly what we expected. Creators have become indispensable political pundits, but there’s still plenty of room at the table for traditional networks, too.

#7423. Are Reddit’s new search ads just an answer engine optimization play?

In a blog post published on November 3, Reddit revealed that it’s testing a new ad product. Alongside a “select group of eligible advertisers,” the social platform is experimenting with paid media posts that show up in its search results.

The new ads will harness Reddit’s “existing ad targeting” to surface relevant product recommendations on search pages. The blog post provided two examples of how that process could work: A search for “espresso station” could show results for coffee machines, beans, and mugs, and a query for “home office equipment” could deliver paid listings for monitors, desks, and chairs.

On their own, the search ads have plenty of utility for brands that want to reach Reddit’s growing community, which includes a large share of Millennial and Gen Z users. At the same time, the new format has intriguing connections to the emerging industry known as answer engine optimization (AEO).

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

AEO is a marketing strategy that uses paid media to affect the referrals made by generative AI models. Reddit was once the king of chatbot referrals; that advantage inspired other platforms to copy its signature layout.

YouTube has since snatched the chatbot referral crown from Reddit, and its ties to AEO strategies are a big reason why. Agencies are working with brands to produce creator content that shows up in future chatbot queries.

Compared to YouTube, Reddit isn’t really a creator hub. Its content is produced by users who typically stay anonymous and stick to text. The type of AEO companies like Zoom are doing on YouTube won’t necessarily work on Reddit.

So as funding continues to pour into the AEO industry, Reddit has to develop its own mechanisms for those marketers. One potential solution is a new video product that resembles TikTok. Those clips can make Reddit more creator-friendly while also retaining control of content that often goes viral on other platforms.

Now, with search ads, Reddit has another solution it can potentially sell to AEO firms. It is letting brands insert themselves on search pages that could be scraped by LLMs. That idea won’t make up the referral gap with YouTube all on its own, but it’s a step in the right direction.

#7421. Netflix might want its new AI search to drum up more “quality” viewership

Netflix‘s new strategy for combating YouTube‘s commanding share of living room TVs is to insist that it’s not the quantity of viewership, but the quality.

And it might be trying to pump up those quality views with a new recommendation tool.

Of course, the times being what they are, the tool is AI.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

AI Discover is intended to curate Netflix’s offerings in a hyperpersonalized manner, so people only see what they like. If this sounds familiar, it’s because Netflix is doing what YouTube, X, and Meta have already done: shunt the responsibility for a quality recommendation algorithm onto viewers and their input.

“There’s more to enjoy and discover on Netflix than ever, but what sounds right for a quiet night in may look different for family movie night or a few spare minutes,” Netflix said in an announcement post. “We’ve spent years refining how you discover, with recommendations tailored to your tastes, from what you Thumbs Up to what you add to ‘My List.’ Now, AI Discover joins the mix as a new way to explore.”

Once a theme is in place, Netflix’s bot brings up a bunch of suggestions, and also additional narrower themes within the first themes. Netflix says there will be a process of “tuning” AI Discover’s recommendations until it “find[s] your next obsession.”

Users who think the bot is getting too far off what they want can refresh the whole deal. Netflix also lets people tell it titles they don’t like.

Unlike the aforementioned social media platforms, Netflix doesn’t seem to have included a ChatGPT-esque discussion aspect to this tool. Users just click through and select what they like, and what they don’t.

Makes sense, since YouTube, Meta, and X have their own in-house chatbots they can shove into everything; Netflix doesn’t have a Gemini or Grok or Muse equivalent, so a yes/no system is its best option. It did partner with OpenAI in 2025 to test an AI search feature that was rumored would replace its regular search function, but that never materialized in full across the service. Maybe this is the version of that idea it ultimately ended up with, sans GPT chatting.

Netflix does say AI Discover is “powered by a new intelligence layer we’ve been building that responds to what members tell us in real time and keeps learning.”

This brings us back to what we said at the top of this article: Netflix is looking for quality viewership. And, well, if it can gather an immense amount of information about viewers’ preferences with this new “intelligence layer,” it might be able to more accurately match them with what they want to watch.

That in turn could drive up the amount of time people spend watching a movie or a TV show–and Netflix might start shooting for average view duration as a way to supercede YouTube.

For now, Netflix’s new AI discovery is only available on TVs in the U.S. (interesting choice), and only in English. Netflix says it won’t appear on kids’ profiles. Per Variety, the streamer plans to expand to more international users in the coming weeks.

You'll do the schlep work other teams don't have time for, digging into a bucket's access pattern, writing the dbt model or Python pipeline that ships the fix, building the cost-vs-revenue mart that answers a margin question once instead of every time, and chasing a number until it reconciles. Strong communication matters as much as technical depth, you'll regularly explain a savings case or a data model's implications to an engineering team, a finance stakeholder, and a leadership audience in the same week.What You'll Be Responsible ForIn this role, you'll:

Find and ship savings across AWS and GCP: Analyze billing, usage, and cost trends to identify opportunities, rightsizing, storage lifecycle policies, data transfer, and spot/auto-scaling. Take ideas from identification through to a realized dollar figure, not just a recommendation.

Build and maintain the FinOps data pipeline: Design and run the BigQuery/dbt models that turn raw billing and usage data (CUR, Storage Lens) into reconciled, trustworthy mart tables, the foundation everything else in FinOps is built on.

Build cost-vs-revenue and customer segmentation models: Model unit economics and margin by product line and customer segment, and extend coverage as new products and segments come online.

Apply data science to cost and usage data: Build forecasting models, detect anomalies statistically rather than by threshold alone, and quantify savings opportunities (e.g. storage lifecycle, request-cost patterns) with rigor a spreadsheet can't match.

Build and maintain cost attribution: Tagging policies, cost allocation, and chargeback/showback so engineering teams can see and own their own spend. This is foundational work other savings work depends on.

Automate cost governance: Build automated cost reporting, anomaly detection, and alerting. Write the scripts and infrastructure-as-code (Python, Terraform, Lambda) that enforce cost policy rather than relying on manual review.

Partner with engineering on architecture decisions: Bring cost into the room early, cost-efficiencies are cheaper to get right at design than to retrofit.

Work with Finance on forecasting and reporting: Support budget tracking and financial KPIs; build dashboards and self-serve analytics engineering and finance can both read.

Have strong AWS expertise and working GCP knowledge, including pricing models, billing structures, and cost optimization mechanics.

Have data engineering depth: dbt, BigQuery (or an equivalent modern warehouse), SQL at scale, and data modeling for analytics (dimensional modeling, incremental models, testing).

Have data science fundamentals: statistical forecasting, anomaly detection, and experimentation, and know when a rigorous model beats a rule of thumb.

Have automation and scripting skills: Python, Terraform/ pulumi, Lambda, or Bash.

Are comfortable with cost/billing tooling: AWS Cost Explorer, Cost & Usage Reports, GCP Billing Reports, and BI/dashboarding (we use Hex).

Have experience with, or are comfortable picking up, Linear and Notion as the system of record for tracking and documenting FinOps work.

Experience with a dedicated cloud cost management platform (e.g. CloudZero, Vantage, or similar) is a plus, not required.

Can analyze cost data and present it clearly to both technical and non-technical audiences.

Have prior experience spanning data analytics, data engineering, or data science in a FinOps, cloud cost management, or cloud governance context.

Are energized by doing the unglamorous, high-leverage work (the schlep) that unblocks other teams, and by working cross-functionally without positional authority.

RELATED ARTICLEIn Medill’s latest State of Local News report, a “festering, 20-year-old problem” looms larger than everSophie CulpepperOctober 22, 2025If you thought last year was bleak, Medill’s annual State of Local News Report is here to ring the alarm bell louder.

What was a “creeping erosion” has now “mushroomed into a full-blown super El Niño-like event for local news, leaving widespread and long-lasting displacement in its wake,” writes Tim Franklin, founding director of the Medill Local News Initiative, in his introduction to this year’s report, released Tuesday. The Northwestern University team’s research “paints a portrait of a local news ecosystem in a state of precarity.”

In the past year, Medill tracked 26 new news deserts, “the largest single-year rise by far since Medill began keeping records five years ago,” Franklin writes. The previous year, only six new news deserts emerged.

Medill’s team says to understand that acceleration, you have to look at where newspapers are disappearing fastest now. While about 70% of the papers that disappeared over the past 20 years were based in urban or suburban communities, in recent years a greater share of newspaper closures have happened in smaller, rural and poorer communities, according to the report.

“When the news disappears in these counties, it stays gone,” the report states.

RELATED ARTICLELast year, Illinois started giving local news outlets tax credits to support journalism jobs. A new report looks at how it’s goingSophie CulpepperFebruary 9, 2026Many of the new news deserts emerged because of small rural papers shuttering in the Midwest. In fact, the report notes that Illinois lost more newspapers than any other state: 30 newspapers shuttered in the state between July 2025 and August 2026, “all small to medium-size outlets.” That means nearly one in five of the 170 newspapers that shuttered in that year was based in Illinois. The state’s losses are especially notable because it enacted one of the first public policies to preserve and grow local journalism jobs in 2024.

“Independent owners of small to midsize newspapers especially were already operating on a knife’s edge,” Brier Dudley writes in his examination of newspaper losses in Illinois. “This past year, their slim margins were squeezed by shrinking revenues and steeply escalating prices for newsprint, fuel and other materials.”

The price of newsprint rose nearly 18% over the past year, Dudley reported, as U.S. mills closed or stopped production of newsprint. That’s about five times the national rate of inflation, he noted. As of April, the United States has just one newsprint producer left.

A few other highlights from this year’s report:

The extreme urban-rural divide: “Virtually all the new news sources are in urban areas, while rural America is increasingly arid news and information territory,” Franklin writes. “And virtually all the philanthropic support for local news is in metro regions.” The report notes that there are fewer than 50 counties in the U.S. “that lack a newspaper but feature an alternative digital or broadcast outlet.” Of the 287 news outlets to start up in the last five years, nearly 80% are in urban areas.

Traffic declines: Digital readership is in “precipitous decline” for many outlets. According to Comscore data from more than 700 local news sites, monthly traffic has dropped by an average of nearly 2 million pageviews, or almost 30%. Meanwhile, traffic to 100 of the largest local newspapers has declined by almost 50% since 2022.

Local TV news: This year, for the first time, Medill’s report included local TV newsrooms. The team identified 678 local commercial TV newsrooms across the country. The overwhelming majority are located in metro areas with existing local news outlets. (“Adding commercial television to the LNI database made little impact on which counties we identify as news deserts,” the team notes.) TV news is already highly consolidated — the five largest owners control more than half of newsrooms, and the 10 largest control 75% — and further consolidation is underway, if Nexstar’s $6.2 billion acquisition of Tegna survives an antitrust lawsuit. The deal would merge the second- and fourth-largest owners of local commercial TV newsrooms.

The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try new things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.

#7414. Ignition, Inc.: MSP Mac Help Desk Guru (work from home)

Ignition is one of the oldest Apple Technical Partners on the planet, and the only fractional IT firm that specializes in the venture-backed technology ecosystem.

Fully Remote · Work from home · Full-time (Eastern or Pacific time zones) · Apple-first

ignitionit.com is a seasoned, Apple-first MSP — in business for almost 30 years — and we're hiring a Help Desk Technician to be the friendly, capable first voice our clients reach when something isn't working. This position is a remote, work-from-home, full-time role.

We've written this as a junior-to-mid-level job description because that's where most great people start on our team. But if you're more seasoned — comfortable in identity, MDM, or security work — don't scroll past. We'd be delighted to find someone who can step in higher up the ladder, and we'll happily talk about a more senior scope and comp if that's you.

Unlike many IT shops, we believe that the technology is the tactic. The actual job is making people feel taken care of. One of our core values is “49% tech support, 51% human support.”

You'll succeed by configuring devices, resetting access, untangling email, and chasing down the gremlin that's been haunting someone's conference room. But you'll know you succeeded when a client exhales and says, “Thank goodness you're on it!” That Warm Fuzzy Feeling™ is the actual product. The green lights on the dashboard are just how we get there.

Onboard a new hire at a fast-growing startup: provision their Mac, set up their Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 accounts, enroll the device in MDM, and make sure day one feels effortless.

Offboard a departing employee cleanly — recover the laptop, revoke access, and close the loop so nothing's left dangling. All boxes checked, ticket notated and closed, client followed up with.

Field a "my email stopped working" ticket that turns out to be a DNS thing, a phishing-filter thing, or a "they changed their password on their phone three weeks ago" thing.

Help a family office or RIA get a touchy Zoom Room or conference-room AV setup behaving before a meeting — over the phone.

Triage the queue so phones get answered fast, emails don't rot, and nobody feels forgotten — even when the honest answer is, “We're on it, but here's the realistic timeline."

⠀ You'll be the front line: helping with what you can, researching what you can't, and pinging the rest of the team when you're genuinely stuck. That last part is a skill, not a weakness — knowing when to ask is half the job.

We're one of the oldest Apple Technical Partners on the planet, and one of the only certified Apple Premier Partners — that’s kinda like getting knighted by the ghost of Steve Jobs. We started where you’d expect to find Macs (creative agencies, non-profits, education) but our primary clients today are cutting-edge, venture-backed AI SaaS startups, VC and private equity firms, registered investment advisors — many of them operating under stringent compliance expectations (SOC 2, SEC). That means we hold ourselves to a higher standard than the scrappy shop we started as. Polished, reliable, security-minded work is the baseline now — but always with a smile!

What hasn't changed: relationships are still our most valuable currency — with clients, with vendors, and with each other. We're a tight, supportive team. We teach each other what we know, cover for each other when life throws a punch, and care a little too much about doing things the right way. We're still a bit weird, and our clients seem to like us that way.

We move fast, priorities shift, it’s not always documented (whatever it is), our tool set and list of supported platforms is sprawling, and some days the to-do list is longer than you'd like. If you can stay warm under pressure, create order out of chaos, learn new stuff fast because you love it, and speak up when you need help, you'll thrive here.

If you need a rigid, fully-documented, never-changes environment where nobody trusts you with admin access, where you will be micro-managed so you never have to wonder whether or not you’re doing the right thing, this isn't it. You’ll have a ton of independence on our team, and freedom to use your best judgment to get the ball over the finish line, but that also means we expect you to be naturally responsible, honest, and highly accountable — to yourself, your teammates, and the clients. As they say, the price of freedom is eternal vigilance.

The tech you'll work with (and grow into)

Apple at the core — macOS, iOS, Apple Business Manager, and MDM (Jamf / Iru / Intune / Workspace ONE / and more)

Yes, PCs too — about one-third of our users are driving Windows

Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 admin consoles

Identity and access — SSO, MFA, and security keys (Okta, Entra ID, Yubikey, and friends)

Lots of other security tools — our stack is constantly evolving and may vary from client to client

The everyday productivity stack — Slack, Zoom, conference-room AV, networking basics (Meraki), and endpoint tooling

⠀ You don't need to know all of this. You need to be the kind of person who wants to. As you grow, there's a clear path into infrastructure administration, project architecture and implementation, and — for the right person — security and compliance work (phishing simulations, endpoint detection, SOC 2 / CIS / SEC readiness, due diligence questionnaire support, etc.). That's where our most senior people live, and it's wide open.

The hard requirements — we won't move forward unless you:

Can work standard business hours in Eastern or Pacific time zones (we currently need both)

Have a quiet home workspace and reliable broadband

Have proven Apple aptitude — you actually use and like the Apple ecosystem

Have at least 5 years of IT support experience on the job.

⠀ Everything else — and this is the longer list, on purpose. We figure technical skills are teachable; character takes a lot longer. So we're looking for someone who:

Genuinely cares — about clients, teammates, and doing right by people

Loves to learn, and proves it in how they spend their time

Reads, and writes clearly — clear writing is clear thinking, and you'll do a lot of it

Stays calm and kind with a frustrated person on the other end of the line

Can tell the difference between good customer service and fantastic customer service, and refuses to settle for the former

Notices when something's being done inefficiently and fixes it (you may boast about it later, that’s fine)

Proofreads their own work (yes, we noticed whether you proofread your application)

Has a sense of humor, and doesn't take themselves too seriously

Our company founder/CEO is headquartered in the Bay Area. We work with innovative, ambitious companies developing AI products. Our team members hold a range of opinions about whether AI is “good or bad” for humans, but at the end of the day, we embrace the plain fact that it is here, we must embrace it to evolve, and our clients increasingly depend on us to help them embrace it, too, to help them evolve and stay competitive.

Our CEO's opinion: AI will not replace human labor any time soon; rather, AI is a new opportunity to either (a) get things done faster, or (b) get a much higher quality of output than before. If you’re an AI tinkerer, great! We want to hear how you’re using it and see your latest vibe project. If you’re allergic to AI or have no interest in learning new habits to work effectively with it, this is not the place for you.

Base salary: Applicants outside the USA will be compensated according to your local employment market. For applicants closer to the junior side who are located in the USA, $50,000–$65,000/yr, depending on experience level and your local geographical price index. With experience, comp goes up from there. Genuinely experienced, more senior candidates can be slotted higher — let's talk.

Type & location: Full-time, work from home, fully remote. Eastern or Pacific time zones.

Benefits: Medical / dental / vision for the employee, 401(k) with employer contribution, 2 weeks of PTO annually to start, and a stipend for your home internet.

The first step is really easy and only takes 10 minutes — no resume, no cover letter, no essays. Here's how:

Take this online Culture Index assessment (about 10 minutes): We use it to screen for people whose natural wiring fits how our team works.

If your profile lines up with what we're looking for, we'll reach out and ask you to complete a 60-minute TestGorilla assessment for critical thinking skills, send us your resume, and maybe a couple of other items.

From there, we conduct between 2-4 video interviews. One of these might be a live technical assessment.

If the Culture Index step feels like a strange way to start a job application — that's kind of the point. Remember the phrase Think Different?

Ignition is an equal opportunity employer. We welcome and will consider all qualified applicants. Good luck in your search — and may the Force be with you!

No forms. Just smart, optimized applications.

Remember every detail and next step, without a meeting bot.

#7413. When Slate went back to its 1996 homepage, it learned some web design lessons for 2026

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“I am a direct traffic girly and I know I’m not alone.”

RELATED ARTICLESlate, now 20 years old, reflects on the value of taking the long view and not chasing digital media trendsShan WangSeptember 23, 2016The fonts are Times New Roman and Arial Narrow, the colors are maroon and mustard, and the cursor is the 8-bit pixel hand. When Slate revived its original 1996 homepage to celebrate its 30th birthday this fall1, the team found a lot to like besides nostalgia.

“I’ve read Slate since 1997, when I finally had access to my own computer at my first job,” Hillary Frey, Slate’s editor-in-chief, told me recently. At the age of 51, she said, “I’m speaking as an old. But I am a direct traffic girly and I know I’m not alone.”

Slate’s homepage has long functioned as a “fossil of what the internet was during that time,” said Ivylise Simones, Slate’s creative director. In 1996, Slate was trying to figure out what a magazine on the internet should even look like; in 2026, it’s among the last general-interest digital-native news sites, and print magazines are dying out. “Salon is one of our only lasting contemporaries,” Frey noted. “There are other sort of fellows from that era, like Feed and Nerve. They’ve been gone for awhile.”

RELATED ARTICLESlate launches a metered paywall to draw more membership revenue from readers, not just listenersSarah ScireMarch 26, 2020In its 30th anniversary campaign, Slate has found its fossil-like nature to be something of a selling point. (It can also be a challenge.) Over the years, the site has published a number of posts about its history and editorial and design choices. A decade ago, then–news editor Chad Lorenz wrote “A history of Slate in nine home pages.” (At launch, Slate articles included page numbers and printing instructions.) A 1998 paywall, Lorenz wrote, was “fortunately” abandoned by 1999. But the paywall returned in 2020. (It was metered at the start, but today it’s dynamic, changing based on user behavior.) For its 30th birthday, the site is running a promotion: a year of access for $19.96.

RELATED ARTICLECan’t read just one: Slate’s daily advice columns are strange, funny, deep, and increasingly a major traffic driver for the siteLaura Hazard OwenJuly 22, 2019“Going back to our roots, there are certain elements we are starting to really love,” Simones said, and she’s thinking about how to include them in the site’s ongoing redesign. She likes the spareness and simplicity of earlier versions of the site, she said, pointing to Reddit and Discord as places that are “more reminiscent of old homepages than the current, very stylized, very gridded layout” found across the internet. A less dense homepage on desktop, she said, is “refreshing.”

“Our editorial guiding light is the mix,” Frey added. Slate has verticals, but they’re not emphasized in the story selection at the top of the homepage; instead, life, politics, and advice stories are mixed together and weighted similarly. “Having an image for every story you share on the homepage is just not necessary,” Simones noted.

Some 1990s-era headline styles still work, too, Frey has found. One of her favorites is a 2002 piece by Slate founding editor Michael Kinsley: “The secret vice of power women.”

“He was writing it about his wife, who found tremendous satisfaction and relaxation in watching police procedurals,” Frey said. “That’s something I still identify with, though most of them now are from Finland and Norway. 100%, this headline would play on the Slate homepage right this second.”

Art courtesy of Slate A wrinkle for 2026: The 1996-inspired homepage had to work on mobile, even though nobody was reading Slate on a phone 30 years ago. [↩]

#7410. Two creators went to NYU’s business school, then decided to make a show about the news

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“Our videos are what we wish we could consume more of.”

The data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

On a September afternoon in Manhattan’s Union Square neighborhood, Shreyas Sinha is sitting on a toilet, wearing a blue suit. Looking into the camera, he asks, “Why is it that everything I’ve been eating this year is giving me diarrhea?”

Sinha is about to link the 2026 cyclospora outbreaks to decades of problems at the Food and Drug Administration. “I’m only allowed to make three diarrhea jokes in this video,” Sinha says. “I live in tyranny.”

The toilet video is one of the tamer stunts that Sinha and his co-creator, Gaurav Srivatchan, have pulled for their YouTube channel, A Show About The News, a weekly deep dive into major business and politics stories (tagline: “Critics are calling it the worst alternative to mainstream media, and those are just the critics I’m related to.”)

In a video about why young people can’t afford to buy homes, Sinha pops out of a cardboard box on the street and takes former New York City mayor Eric Adams to a studio apartment filled with men. Other recent videos include a 45-minute interview on the street with former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci, an explainer on prediction market ads, and a rap music video on why retirement investments are safer than get-rich-quick schemes.

Sinha, 25, and Srivatchan, 22, met in 2023 when they were students at New York University’s Stern School of Business. They teamed up to make short vertical explainer videos, but those didn’t take off as much as they’d hoped. In 2024, Sinha quit his finance job to pursue A Show About The News full-time, and they transitioned to creating long-form deep dives with a dash of their own humor.

I chatted with Sinha and Srivatchan about how they launched their media careers, how they use humor to explain the news, and what they think business opportunities are for creators today. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Tameez: Why did you start creating news videos? Sinha: Gaurav and I started making videos together during the spring 2023 semester, when I was a senior at NYU and he was a freshman. I had been doing a newsletter for a while, I had been doing stand-up comedy for a few years, and I was interning at CNN. It seemed like everything was [pointing to], “Hey, you should start making short-form videos.” And then Gaurav was like, “Hey, I’m actually really good at editing videos.” We were not really thinking of it as a YouTube channel, but as making short-form stories. At the time, we were called Fifty50 Media. We were all about trying to distill the world into bipartisan perspectives. We eventually started focusing more on deeper-dive stories. We renamed ourselves to A Show About the News. It’s very easy to put out a political opinion that goes viral, but we really wanted to focus on good stories. Eventually, we started making videos for Morning Brew, and we joined Morning Brew full-time as a franchise in August 2025.

I had been doing a newsletter for a while, I had been doing stand-up comedy for a few years, and I was interning at CNN. That’s one of the reasons we started working on long-form videos. We made another and another, and then they were like, “You guys should just do this for us.” Srivatchan: Morning Brew provided us access to this office. It’s great to not meet under a lofted bed in Shreyas’ apartment. Sinha: They’re an excellent partner [because] they believe in allowing editorial control to be with the person who makes the video. We’re not going into meetings asking, can we do this topic next week? It’s a very high-trust environment, which, from talking to other people who work at other media companies, is extremely rare. Tameez: You guys both left careers in finance to do this full-time. Sinha: It was an economically stupid decision, but I knew that if I failed now, I would be young enough to start again. It’s easy to have the golden handcuffs of waiting until the right time, but there is never a right time. It was taking a bet on myself and someone who I really trusted. Still, our videos were getting 12 views at that time; it wasn’t as if something took off and it was like, “Okay, this can pay our bills.”

Srivatchan: I had the advantage of being younger. [Shreyas left] a full-time job. I did my summer internship in consulting and got my return offer, but it was a lot less of a risk for me, personally. It obviously helped that we had some backing from Morning Brew. Tameez: Why is making A Show About the News important now? How does it fit into the larger information ecosystem? Sinha: What we do, in the context of where we went to school, is the equivalent of becoming ballerinas. All of my friends are investment bankers in private equity or in consulting. That is the tried and true method [for NYU Stern graduates]. If you tell people, “Hey, I’m not recruiting for banking, I’m thinking of doing consulting,” they look at you like you just said you want to be an art major. When we said we were going to build a media company, it was truly mind-boggling for people. I loved what Fareed Zakaria did, what Ezra Klein did, but my favorite people when I was a kid were Jon Stewart and John Oliver, Hasan Minhaj and Seth Meyers and Conan O’Brien and Nathan Fielder. I knew I wasn’t going to be a great stand-up comedian, I wasn’t going to be a great writer, but maybe I could combine those to make a job out of it. It’s easy to pat ourselves on the back and say there’s a lot of garbage out there. But also, it has never been a better time to be an independent creator. If we both wanted to go into media today, we would be grabbing water for hosts who get paid $60 million a year. Instead, we actually get to put our own ideas out there.

It’s easy to pat ourselves on the back and say there’s a lot of garbage out there. But also, it has never been a better time to be an independent creator. If we both wanted to go into media today, we would be grabbing water for hosts who get paid $60 million a year. Instead, we actually get to put our own ideas out there.

Tameez: Tell me about your workflow, from video ideation to posting. Sinha: We don’t do short-form clips [from longer videos]. We script our shorts. That takes a ton of time. [But] long-form is the priority. It takes much more time, but you really get to have a relationship with the audience. Srivatchan: When it comes to shorts, either Shreyas or I will have something that really interests us for the week. We start scripting it, then we switch the scripts and each of us does a pass on the other’s. Then we revise them and film them. That takes roughly two out of five workdays. We spend the rest of the time on long-form. We’re also doing a weekly livestream to discuss the headlines with the audience and build that audience connection. So our output is two native short-form, one long-form, and one live stream per week.

It takes much more time, but you really get to have a relationship with the audience. We start scripting it, then we switch the scripts and each of us does a pass on the other’s. Then we revise them and film them. That takes roughly two out of five workdays. We start scripting it, then we switch the scripts and each of us does a pass on the other’s. Then we revise them and film them. That takes roughly two out of five workdays. We spend the rest of the time on long-form.

We’re also doing a weekly livestream to discuss the headlines with the audience and build that audience connection. So our output is two native short-form, one long-form, and one live stream per week.

Sinha: Do we actually have something new to say about it? There’s no point in making a video that someone else has already made.

A lot of people have made videos about how people aren’t having kids anymore. That doesn’t mean we wouldn’t [cover that topic], but we need to have something new to say. In our video, we talked about how governments have spent tens of billions of dollars but it hasn’t resulted in any more babies. We talked about demographic trends and got into studies. We brought in a bunch of 19- and 20-year-olds and asked them why they’re not having more sex. Then we went to a bunch of older people and were like, “So, you guys were doing it hella in the 90s. What’s the secret? Let’s give it to these kids.”

Sinha: We try to be funny, maybe to a deficit. In one of our worst-performing videos, we had a guy come in on an inflatable horse. Gaurav was wearing a Will Smith mask and slapped me. But sometimes it really works. We filmed this thing where we were having a shootout with Abraham Lincoln as he smoked a vape. That did great for us.

I listen to a lot of podcasts of serious, smart people. The way they talk, I’m like, how are you not ripping your hair off right now? How are you not just slamming your head against your desk?

Srivatchan: We have all these sources that we regularly read. For a lot of politics and inside scoops on Capitol Hill, Politico is great. For more niche stories, ProPublica is great. Each source has its own strength. We send stuff to each other all the time.

Once we’re in the research phase of a video, we do everything possible to learn about what the scope of the video is and what sources and articles can fall into that.

Sinha: We do a lot of our own fact-checking. Corrections often occur in the way of Gaurav coming to me and being like, “Shreyas, you moron, you said this and it’s actually this.” Then we record a voiceover, or we change it in the captions, or we just put it up as text.

Sinha: If you go on YouTube right now, high production quality is the expectation. It’s not like when I was young and my favorite YouTubers were clearly filming in their bedrooms. There’s so much money that is being invested into it, which is awesome, but if you want to have authentic relationships with your audiences, you need to do more.

Srivatchan: Earlier this year, TBPN [Technology Business Programming Network] was sold to OpenAI for $100 million. Their whole thing was live-streaming. They didn’t get that many viewers concurrently on their livestreams — everything was clips, targeting a very specific niche — but we saw how they grew through clips.

Sinha: When we started making these videos, I was writing articles on the side and freelancing so that I could pay rent. Eventually, this was able to pay rent.

By no means are we rich. But we really believe in the business model of digital media. It’s important to incentivize people to invest in media that is fact-checked, that is telling stories that are new and not just polarizing or viral for virality’s sake. You can’t ask people to only think of [media] as a charity expenditure or as a nonprofit, because those are the first things that go away when the market goes down, and the first thing people are going to stop cutting checks to if they don’t see the ROI.

We spend most of our time thinking about content, but it’s important to be creative about our business models. We always tell ourselves not to think about ourselves as employees or YouTubers, but to keep reminding ourselves that we’re founders of a startup that is trying to do something for the world.

The prevailing narrative that news media is doing poorly is because news media for generations was run by journalists, and that was fine because they could get cable carrier fees. But the reason they were able to do that was because they had a monopoly. You could only watch CNN, CBS, and ABC News because that’s all you had.

[I asked Sinha and Srivatchan to answer a few final questions via email. Their answers are below.]

Sinha: It’s hard to say what’s legacy and what’s new these days. Morning Brew has never had a TV broadcast or print media arm, but it’s owned by a media conglomerate, Axel Springer. Other news companies, from CNN to The Wall Street Journal, have pretty successful social media presences and journalists who’ve made a name for themselves.

The crisis for news companies that dominated in the 20th century is that they relied on fixed distribution: cable, broadband, local stations, and papers. A random Joe couldn’t get their ideas placed in those, so the competition for viewership was highly limited.

Today, competition is high. Legacy journalists who struggle often blame the changing tides of information consumption, when in reality they’re just struggling to compete for attention. Many have been successful in making the transition, so we don’t think it’s fair to paint all of legacy journalism as having something to learn from news creators. But our message overall would be that traditional news shouldn’t blame consumers for not maintaining their expensive newspaper and cable subscriptions, but instead [should] figure out how to compete and win in this new age.

Srivatchan: For journalists who have been successful in their careers but want to transition to social media, we think they severely underestimate how well-prepared they are to make the jump. They’ve already been writing strong articles and hooks to get people to click. We think journalists underestimate how that skill can translate on a platform like YouTube, where everything is dependent on the packaging that gets someone to click on your video.

Often, when someone from traditional media starts a new Instagram or YouTube page, they make very lo-fi content, talking to their phone with their headphones mic. I think they see influencers doing that and think viewers want authenticity. That works for some people, but our view is that investing in strong production is the baseline expectation on social media.

Instead of seizing the social media opportunity, often, legacy journalism is falling into the trap of liquidating its reputation for more attention and to better monetize its declining assets. It’s partnering with gambling apps — CNN’s partnership with Kalshi, or [Dow Jones’] with Polymarket — and inviting inflammatory internet voices rather than the trusted ones that educate.

#7407. Google’s News AI pilot expands to over 400 publications, including U.S. local news outlets

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

In December, Google launched its News AI pilot program, which licenses content from select publishers and uses it to test new AI features in Google News. On Thursday, the company announced that the program has added new partnerships, bringing the total number of publications in the pilot to more than 400 worldwide.

At launch, the program partnered with international publishers like The Guardian, El País, The Times of India, and The Washington Post. More publications are now coming on board, including CNN, The Financial Times, Axios, and Forbes.

RELATED ARTICLEDiscover isn’t the only place Google is experimenting with AI-generated snippetsAndrew DeckJanuary 26, 2026As part of the expansion, the program has also added local news publishers across the U.S., including The Post and Courier in Charleston, South Carolina; Oil City News in Casper, Wyoming; the Illinois- and Iowa-based newspaper chain Shaw Media; and the nonprofit newsroom The Texas Tribune.

“People’s information consumption habits are changing, and we want to make sure publishers of all sizes, local newsrooms included, can navigate these shifts,” Brianna Puccini Duff, a spokesperson for Google, said in a statement to Nieman Lab.

Google declined to comment on the exact terms of the deals. However, Duff clarified that the News AI pilot does not operate on a “pay-per-value” model, meaning publishers are not compensated based on how much their content contributes to an AI-generated output. (The pay-per-value model is part of a parallel program that pays publishers for content surfaced in AI Overviews, AI Mode, and Gemini, according to a recent report by Digiday.)

With the News AI pilot, publishers are instead paid to provide content that appears in experimental AI-powered features. That includes “story previews” — in-depth, AI-generated article summaries of recent stories that may show up on a publisher’s Google News page. Here’s a Washington Post example, with a disclaimer noting the copy is AI-generated and “may include mistakes.”

An AI-generated “story preview” on the Google News page for The Washington Post

Another test feature is “audio briefing,” a customizable, AI-generated podcast in the Google News app that stitches together daily headlines. Users can select the topics they’re most interested in hearing about, including “World,” “Gaming,” or “Sports” news. The feature includes citations that link to articles mentioned in the briefing.

#7406. A new report argues newsrooms need to do more experiments — like, the kind with randomization and results

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Mississippi Today had a question. Did the stories around its Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative reporting affect the way those investigations were received?

It’s the kind of question local newsrooms can’t easily test on their own. But researchers from Local NExT Lab at Syracuse University could.

In a national survey, 1,768 adults were shown the same investigation surrounded by a different mix of stories. In one, the investigation was shown alongside positive community stories. (Think: “How a local fossil park changed science history.”) In another, the investigation was featured alongside other investigative stories.

The investigation was rated more accurate, important, and relevant when it was surrounded by community-focused stories, not other investigative stories. (Audience reaction to a third story mix, where the investigation was surrounded by stories about legislation, was not consistent.)

The result was described in the first report from the Local NExT Lab. Joshua Darr, director of the lab and associate professor at Syracuse University, believes that although dashboards and engagement analytics are “very important tools” for newsrooms, they aren’t enough.

“Engagement data can’t tell you what caused audiences to engage, settle a hunch, or isolate your contribution,” the report reads. “Randomization can.”

“The key word there is ’caused,'” Darr added in an email. “Without randomization, you can tell when engagement is up or down or if a particular story is doing well, but it’s hard to know exactly why that is happening.”

RELATED ARTICLESearching for gold: Making sense of academic research about journalismAngie Drobnic HolanApril 27, 2023At Nieman Lab, we often hear from both sides of academic-practitioner partnerships. Researchers wonder why newsrooms don’t pay attention to their findings or fail to respond to their overtures about experiments. Publishers, editors, and journalists, meanwhile, tell me they don’t have time to read dense and jargon-filled academic papers. They can be annoyed by requests to spend time or resources they don’t have. And it’s not always fun to be someone else’s test subject.

When partnering with Local NExT Lab, Darr emphasized, the local newsrooms don’t have to commit money or manpower. They agree to two or three conversations. The researchers listen and then design, field, and analyze the experiments. In return, the newsrooms get their ideas tested and causal evidence.

In another experiment, the Local NExt Lab found that Instagram Reels including reporters’ faces drove the most interest and engagement, but when it came to clicking “follow,” profiles that looked like traditional news brands won out. Respondents chose to follow newsrooms (in this case New Orleans Public Radio) more often than reporter-named accounts.

The first batch of tests was funded by the W.K. Kellogg Foundation. Additional support from the American Journalism Project will allow for further tests on a larger cohort next year. The full report is here.
