#7360. Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Meta’s new commercial terms will go into effect three weeks later than initially planned.

RELATED ARTICLELegal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changesAndrew DeckOctober 17, 2026Meta has delayed the effective date of its new terms of service for business accounts to November 20 in the face of mounting pressure from the global news industry.

Nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15. They would allow for the mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. Virtually every news organization has at least one business account. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.”

The terms were previously set to take effect on October 30, with no way to opt out, setting off an outcry from news publishers, politicians, and press associations on both sides of the Atlantic.

“We are extending the effective date of our updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms to November 20 to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab in a statement Friday.

A Meta spokesperson said on October 17 that the company revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”

As of October 23, Meta has made no other changes to the terms aside from the implementation date. No versions of the terms include language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

“Publishers should always be concerned about tech companies attempting to take content for free, and should assume that Meta is taking this additional time to either find a new way to try to mislead publishers into granting Meta free access to valuable copyrighted content or finally give up in the face of pressure,” said Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “Publishers don’t need more PR statements or explanations. They need Meta to keep its hands off their copyrighted material and respect publishers’ terms of service.”

“I don’t think that repeating the same non-explanations for another three weeks will make much difference,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, added. “But maybe they’ll use the time to come up with better explanations.”

Thomas Höppner, a professor and attorney specializing in competition law in Germany, told Nieman Lab that “Meta’s conduct constitutes a prima facie infringement of European Union competition law, and a textbook case for imposing interim measures.”

The postponement could be a legal strategy that the company is exploring, he said.

“My fear is that this is merely a measure by Meta to reduce the risk of court actions for interim measures,” Höppner said. “If affected parties wait too long from the day of knowledge of the changes [until] the filing of an action, a court will assume that the matter cannot be urgent — and deny interim relief on this ground…Under some jurisdictions, a platform needs to give business users appropriate warning before implementing measures. It may well be that Meta just tries to reduce the risk of losing on the ground not having sufficiently informed business users about its new terms.”

News publishers and press associations have called on regulators to intervene before the terms take effect, and on Meta to include specific language about respecting publishers’ crawling preferences.

On Thursday, the News/Media Alliance in the United States sent a letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, demanding that the company suspend the terms before October 30. The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) sent a similar letter to Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan on the same day.

Multiple European press associations signed a joint letter to the European Commission, citing potential violations of the Digital Markets Act and calling for intervention. Earlier this week, two German publisher associations called on the European Commission to prohibit the new terms from going into effect until a complete review has been conducted.

In the United Kingdom, the Competition and Market Authority sent a formal letter to Meta to discuss the terms. In a parliamentary committee session on Tuesday, executive director Will Hayter said he had a meeting scheduled with the company on Wednesday to learn more about the terms.

“The CMA has been in urgent discussions with Meta this week on this important issue,” a CMA spokesperson said on Friday. “Meta has now paused implementation until 20 November. We will continue to scrutinize these terms and engage with Meta and others as we consider our next steps.”

Theo Bamber, chief executive of the U.K’s News Media Association, wrote on LinkedIn on Friday that “this delay is welcome, but it is a pause not a solution.”

RELATED ARTICLEMeta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts sayAndrew DeckOctober 15, 2026“What needs to happen next is for the Competition and Markets Authority, and other regulators around the world, to secure clear, public commitments from Meta to abandon the offending elements of the new Terms before they take effect,” Bamber said.

9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

A Google Lighthouse update changes how PageSpeed Insights simulates page loads, which can raise lab scores on pages that haven't changed.

PageSpeed Insights is now using Lighthouse 13.6.0, which was released Oct. 27. This version of Lighthouse changes how it simulates how long a page takes to load.

Chrome’s Web Performance Developer Advocate, Barry Pollard, has stated on Bluesky that the updated version of PageSpeed Insights with Lighthouse 13.6.0 is now available. He said this improves the simulated FCP (First Contentful Paint) and the simulated LCP (Largest Contentful Paint), both of which Pollard says will be more accurate than before and generally result in higher scores.

A page may receive a different PageSpeed Insights score without anything on it changing, due to the change in the test. Pollard also said that websites heavily dependent on JavaScript would be more likely to see an impact from the updated test.

Pollard quoted a developer who had posted about how single-page apps (SPAs) had seen a big improvement in their results since the Lighthouse update, citing react.dev. He opened his post stating, “True!”, then added:

“Note this is not SPA-specific (and unrelated to other SPA things we’ve been working on), but more likely to impact JS-heavy sites.”

The experimental soft navigation metrics in Chrome that I wrote about back in October are a separate way of measuring user experience. The data comes from real Chrome users through the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX) and Lighthouse uses a simulated test.

By default, Lighthouse will load a page at full speed and then estimate how it would load on a slower connection. The throttling docs say that this simulated throttling matches PageSpeed Insights’ setup.

The release notes for version 13.6.0 of Lighthouse list several changes to Lantern, which is the simulation behind those estimates, aimed at improving its accuracy.

Lighthouse 13.5 used each request’s fetch priority to decide whether or not it blocked rendering. In 13.6, Lantern uses Chrome’s own render-blocking label for each request (and falls back to using priority only when that label is missing).

A second change applies when the LCP element is text that appears in the same frame as the page’s first content. Lantern now estimates that LCP from the same requests and page tasks it uses for FCP instead of from a set that can include every request made before LCP.

Ivan Akulov showed in a GitHub issue how the old simulation handled a test page created with Framer whose only content above the fold was text, so one element counted as both FCP and LCP. Lighthouse reported much later LCP than FCP for that text. Even though preloading the page’s JavaScript modules improved interactive time for the real page, they caused simulated LCP to be worse.

Pollard thanked Akulov in a reply, saying he “kicked off some of these improvements.” The Lighthouse team closed the issue as completed in the Lantern upgrade listed in the 13.6 release notes.

Lighthouse 13.6 has also updated the Agentic Resource Discovery (ARD) audit from Lighthouse 13.5, which I covered in September. When Lighthouse 13.5 was released, it looked for an ARD manifest under the old ai-catalog names even though the spec had changed to ard.json. So if your website only used the new name but you didn’t include a line in your robots.txt file called Agentmap, it would show as Not Applicable.

With this update, Lighthouse 13.6 will look for an Agentmap line, a rel="ard" link tag or Link header and /.well-known/ard.json prior to looking for the ai-catalog names. And if Lighthouse 13.6 finds the manifest only at an ai-catalog location, it will note that ARD consumers are not required to check there.

The performance score listed for your page in PageSpeed Insights is based on data generated by Lighthouse. According to Google’s PageSpeed Insights documentation, lab data are results of a simulated load using a single device running on a fixed set of network conditions. They note that “having good lab data does not necessarily mean real-user experiences will also be good.”

Field data (also shown in the same report) represents real visits to your website within the last 28 days, as reported by CrUX. Each PageSpeed Insights report includes the version of Lighthouse used to generate results, next to the emulated device.

PageSpeed Insights scores from before and after the Lighthouse 13.6 update weren’t measured with the same simulation. Part of a higher lab score on a page you just optimized may come from the new version, and charts that track lab scores over time may show a jump at the switch to 13.6.

Before reporting an improvement, check that both reports name the same Lighthouse version, and compare the field data.

Lighthouse’s release notes say its team expects 13.6 to ship in the DevTools of Chrome 159, which is now in Chrome’s desktop Dev channel and in Canary. As of Nov. 2, Chrome’s release schedule lists Chrome 159 for stable release on Dec. 8.

An open issue on Lighthouse’s GitHub is also looking into cases where Lantern’s simulated LCP runs far above measured LCP, using large JavaScript and SPA sites as examples.

#7355. I went looking for the source of one little statistic. That was easier said than done.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The claim: 75% of your emotions are generated by smell. It had to come from somewhere, right?

Apparently, 75% of your emotions are generated by smell.

Or that’s what the internet says, anyway. The statistic appears everywhere from marketing books and articles to academic papers about the power of scent. As a perfumer (someone who creates fragrances) and journalist who writes about these things, I came across it several times, and when I finally wanted to cite it for an article about the impact of scent on mood and memory, I went looking for the original research.

This wasn’t a totally new experience for me. One time, while working on a workplace story as the editor of a hospitality trade magazine, I couldn’t find the source of an employee retention statistic, so I wrote the people who included it in a study. They wrote back to say they had no idea what I was talking about.

In this case, there was no such dead end. I followed link after link, figuring surely I would get to the bottom of it, but every source pointed to another source, which pointed to another, and somehow none of them led to the original research I was looking for.

I asked ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Claude for help. They gave me links to wellness blogs, aromatherapy companies, and authoritative-looking PDF reports. But as I ruled each one out as the original source, the answers became more circular, and the trail ate itself.

Me: Where did the statistic that 75% of emotions are generated by smell come from?

Google Gemini The Sense of Smell Institute.

Gemini: There isn’t a specific study. The statistic was popularized through scent marketing research.

Gemini: Martin Lindstrom’s 2005 book Brand Sense.

Me: Does the book contain the original research?

Gemini: Lindstrom commissioned extensive research into sensory branding through the research firm Millward Brown.

Me: Does that research establish that 75 percent of emotions are generated by smell?

Gemini: Would you like to know how lavender and citrus can influence your mood?

Lindstrom did look like a real lead. Several writers and businesses traced the number to the Danish author’s 2005 book Brand Sense: Sensory Secrets Behind the Stuff We Buy. Simon & Schuster’s page for the book says it outright: “Research shows that a full 75% of our emotions are in fact generated by what we smell.” Aha!

I bought the book and read it. While there is talk of emotions and the senses, the number isn’t in there.

Next, I wrote to Lindstrom’s company asking them to point me toward the original research. They sent me a link to a copy of Brand Sense and told me I would find the research in the book.

I tried another route. Brand Sense was based in large part on an international study by market research company Millward Brown. The 75% figure has been attributed directly to that research. So I went looking for the Millward Brown study. But I couldn’t find it anywhere.

There were other questions: Does the stat even make scientific sense? How would you measure the percentage of emotions generated by smell? Do people with no sense of smell experience 75% fewer emotions? And what about emotions that seem to have nothing to do with the senses at all, like grief over someone’s death, a breakup, or anxiety over losing your job?

I asked Kristen Lindquist, a social and affective neuroscientist and psychology professor at Ohio State University who studies emotion. She had never heard of the statistic.

“I imagine if somebody had done that study I would be aware of it,” she told me.

There is a relationship between smell and emotion, and it may be possible to measure something like this, she said. Researchers could, for example, ask people throughout the day how they’re feeling and whether what they’re feeling is related to something they’re seeing, hearing, touching or smelling. But that still wouldn’t make emotion the product of one sense. “Emotions really arise from all of our sensations,” Lindquist said, including signals from within our bodies. Our brains process all of that information together to figure out what is happening and what it means for us.

RELATED ARTICLERepetition makes climate misinformation feel more true — even for those who back climate scienceYangxueqing Mary JiangAugust 12, 2024There’s a name for the particular way an unsupported claim can acquire the appearance of fact through citation: citogenesis. Coined by Randall Munroe in an XKCD comic, the term describes the process by which an unsupported claim gets repeatedly cited until the citations themselves make it look like truth.

I called Jodi Schneider, an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison Information School whose research includes scientific evidence and citation integrity, to talk about it. I sent her the 75% statistic, and she went looking for the source herself.

“It was not a casual ‘Let me look for 20 minutes, and there it is,'” she told me. “I would find a thing, [it] would go to something else, and that would be a dead end.”

The problem, Schneider said, is that repeating a claim is much easier than investigating it. “Somebody says something, it sounds like a thing you’d like to know or repeat, and you don’t trace it back to where it came from. You just pass it on.” Then repetition becomes the “evidence,” and “if you hear the same thing from multiple places, it’s harder to question.”

This psychological phenomenon is known as the illusory truth effect: We’re more likely to believe information we’ve encountered before. The effect was first demonstrated in the 1970s and has since been replicated many times. More unsettlingly, research has found that repetition can make a false claim seem more believable even when it contradicts something we know to be true.

In other words, seeing the same statistic everywhere doesn’t just make it look well sourced; it makes it feel true.

It’s hard to fully check every claim. Writers build arguments from dozens of pieces of information, and tracing each one all the way back to its origin can take an absurd amount of time.

Newsrooms have spent years cutting staff and budgets, including the fact-checkers and copy editors whose job was to catch this kind of thing. At the same time, the volume of information journalists have to sort through has exploded. Finding a source for a claim can take seconds. Establishing where it actually came from can take hours (or an eternity).

Meanwhile, the consequences of not checking facts compound. Once a bad claim gets published, it becomes another source for the next journalist, another search result for the next reader and another apparent confirmation that the claim must be true.

AI is making that problem worse. It repeats the same unsupported claims while stripping away some of the clues that might otherwise make us suspicious of the source.

“The polish that generative AI can put on just about anything is already a challenge,” Schneider said. More importantly, “Generative AI is really, really good at being persuasive, even if the claims inside the persuasion have no basis in reality.”

Most people are not going to track a statistic through six articles, buy the book everyone cites, email the author, and start calling academics. They don’t have the time or energy for that, and they shouldn’t have to do it anyway. One of journalism’s roles is to provide information that’s more reliable than TikTok or whatever nonsense Google Gemini spits out.

When we get it wrong, we don’t just add another bad source to the pile. We give the claim credibility and put it in front of more people. And once they’ve seen it, the illusory truth effect suggests they’re more likely to believe it the next time. (Research has also found that repeated misinformation is more likely to be repeated than new misinformation, and can continue to influence people even after it has been corrected.)

Nobody is going to die because they believe smell generates 75 percent of their emotions. But replace that claim with one about a vaccine, a war, an election or a medical treatment and the same failure becomes considerably less benign.

That’s why the difference between finding a source and finding the source matters. I found hundreds of sources for the 75% statistic. I still haven’t found the source. That doesn’t mean it’s not out there.

Can you find the source of the 75% stat? Email [email protected].

#7353. The Independent Journalism Atlas looks at “wells” and “springs” in news deserts

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

What do we mean when we talk about news deserts?

The term has become a shorthand for areas devoid of local news coverage. But a new essay from the Independent Journalism Atlas recalls that when Penny Abernathy popularized the term through her research, she used it to describe a more nuanced picture:

Things grow in a desert, she told Medill’s Tim Franklin in 2024, just not as abundantly. Asked why she didn’t say “news vacuum,” she answered, “There’s news; it’s just not necessarily the quality and the quantity of what you would find elsewhere.” RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026To show what information can look like in news deserts, the Independent Journalism Atlas — an initiative that aims to “[document] independent creators who inform, educate, and advance public knowledge outside traditional media structures,” cofounded by Liz Kelly Nelson, Justin Bank, and 2025 Nieman Fellow Ryan Kellett — took a closer look at 46 of the 238 news desert counties identified in this year’s State of Local News report from Medill. RELATED ARTICLEMany people who live in “local news deserts” don’t feel deprived of local news, study findsLaura Hazard OwenFebruary 10, 2026“Look at the ground and news moves like water,” writes Bank. “It doesn’t stop at a county line. It runs off the surface, sinks underground and comes up wherever someone digs.” The team found that “in more places than the desert map shows, someone has picked up a shovel.” (That might help explain why people who live in news deserts don’t feel deprived of local news.) The team identifies a few patterns in how information looks and travels in news deserts, including “surface” information, wells, and springs. Posts from the local sheriff, weather alerts, and obituaries from the funeral home are all examples of “surface” information that “runs off,” Bank writes, typically telling you what happened without telling you why. Wells are newsrooms that form when a local paper shutters. The team points to the Anaconda Weekly Review in Deer Lodge County, Montana, as an example of a well appearing in a county Medill identified as a news desert. Springs, meanwhile, are “harder to spot” than wells because they’re smaller and more ad hoc. The Independent Journalism Atlas applies this label to efforts like the Gallatin County Board Illinois Unofficial Facebook page, which livestreams the board’s public meetings and posts its agendas. The team also paid attention to coverage of news deserts by outlets in neighboring counties. They found high school sports are often a gateway to coverage, pointing to a channel covering southern Illinois high school sports that interviewed the principal in Harrisburg, the seat of Saline County, another news desert county. RELATED ARTICLEUniversities are mapping where local news outlets are still thriving — and where gaps persistCorey HutchinsJanuary 16, 2025In recent years, efforts to “map” local news through different lenses have proliferated. The Independent Journalism Atlas is one such effort, focused on news creators. A better understanding of information sources in news deserts matters, Bank argues, because “you can’t tend a basin you haven’t mapped.” Read the full essay here.

Wells are newsrooms that form when a local paper shutters. The team points to the Anaconda Weekly Review in Deer Lodge County, Montana, as an example of a well appearing in a county Medill identified as a news desert.

Springs, meanwhile, are “harder to spot” than wells because they’re smaller and more ad hoc. The Independent Journalism Atlas applies this label to efforts like the Gallatin County Board Illinois Unofficial Facebook page, which livestreams the board’s public meetings and posts its agendas.

The team also paid attention to coverage of news deserts by outlets in neighboring counties. They found high school sports are often a gateway to coverage, pointing to a channel covering southern Illinois high school sports that interviewed the principal in Harrisburg, the seat of Saline County, another news desert county.

9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Google's John Mueller clarified whether site owners can use robots.txt to block Googlebot from downloading specific resources that users see.

Google’s John Mueller answered a question about whether it’s okay to block Googlebot from indexing an age-verification popup that website visitors are required to see. His answer offers some clarity about whether it’s okay to purposely hide some kinds of content from Googlebot and explains how site owners can do it.

Google requires publishers to allow Googlebot to crawl everything that a user might see but that wasn’t always the case. There was a time in the early days of SEO where SEOs blocked Google from downloading JavaScript and CSS files in order to optimize the crawl budget and encourage better website indexing.

But there came a time when Google began rendering web pages and subsequently required site owners to allow Googlebot to download all resources that a user would see. Some sites that continued to block Google from downloading critical resources temporarily lost their rankings.

So the question about whether it’s okay to block Google from indexing a popup is reasonable.

The SEO asked on Reddit whether it’s okay to use robots.txt to prevent Googlebot from indexing an age-verification popup that a website is legally required to display to visitors.

The person described a hypothetical website that loads an age-verification popup from a separate domain through an API. The question was whether blocking Googlebot from crawling that external domain would prevent the popup from being rendered.

“Say I have a website websiteA.com – for legal reasons it has an age verification pop up that sits on a separate domain and is inserted on the page via an API. Lets call it verificationpopup.com

Lets say I wanted to block Google from seeing this – if I added a disallow on verificationpopup.com/robots.txt would that prevent Google from rendering the pop up?

(this is purley a hypothetical and apologies for the stupid Q, I am not very tech minded)”

Mueller confirmed that using robots.txt to prevent Googlebot from rendering the age-verification popup would generally work. He also suggested an alternative approach that involves blocking a JavaScript file responsible for loading the popup.

“That would generally work. If you’re using a specific JS script file to do this, you could also disallow that specific javascript file via robots.txt. (If you only have one JS file that does a bunch of things, I wouldnt’ do that”

Mueller’s response indicates that Google’s algorithms may be looser than it used to be, at least toward something like this age verification popup. His answer confirmed that site owners can use robots.txt to prevent Googlebot from rendering an age-verification popup, even when the popup is displayed to website visitors.

He returned hours later to elaborate in more detail about two ways to accomplish this, addressing two ways the popup is loaded and which resources the site owner can control.

Mueller explained that the first approach involves blocking Googlebot from crawling the external domain that provides the age-verification popup.

In the situation of an external domain that’s the source of the resource that needs blocking, the external domain’s robots.txt can disallow crawling and Googlebot will not fetch those resources and therefore cannot use them to render the popup. Mueller said that this is common with resources related to advertising where a JavaScript file responsible for showing ads is blocked by robots.txt.

the embedded site’s content is blocked by robots.txt. If you embed content from verificationpopup-com on your site (say via iframe or by calling a script on verificationpopup-com, etc), and verificationpopup-com disallows all crawling, then crawlers that follow robots.txt (like Googlebot) would not fetch that content, and would not use it in rendering.

This is how many ads services work. Googlebot wouldn’t crawl these URLs like a separate page, but it would try to fetch them during the course of rendering, and if robots.txt blocks it, then it doesn’t fetch the content, and can’t use it. You need to make sure that your pages still load when those URLs are not fetched, but for something like this, that’s usually not a problem.

Your site uses a specific JS file to load this, and you block that yourself. For example, perhaps you use a “load-verification-popup.js” file to do this. If you block that page with robots.txt on your site, then the script won’t be loaded during rendering (blocked by robots.txt).

In my experience, this is less common, but it’s an option. If the robots.txt on verificationpopup-com is not something you can influence, you’d need to do this, if you wanted to prevent it from being visible/used during rendering.”

So to recap, the second approach involves blocking a JavaScript file that’s used to load the popup that’s on another domain where using a robots.txt is not an option.

The interesting part of Mueller’s answer is that he confirmed a way to deliberately prevent Googlebot from rendering an age-verification popup that human visitors are required to see.

He also explained that the website must continue to load properly when Googlebot cannot fetch the blocked resources. For an age-verification popup like the one described in the question, he indicated that this is usually not a problem.

The overall takeaway is that it’s okay to use robots.txt to prevent Googlebot from downloading and rendering an age-verification popup, even though human visitors are required to see it. Mueller’s answer shows that website owners exercise some control over which resources Googlebot uses during rendering, including resources that are a part of the experience presented to visitors.

Democratic Senator Adam Schiff of California is urging Meta not to implement its forthcoming commercial terms on November 20, his office announced Tuesday.

In a letter sent to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Schiff called on the company to respond by Monday, November 2 with the specific steps it will take to address user concerns.

“Forcing publishers to choose between surrendering their off-platform IP or forfeiting a primary channel of public communication is a gross abuse of Meta’s power as a powerful platform with critical access to consumers,” Schiff wrote. “Meta must not nullify federal IP protections and fair market competition through the unilateral insertion of fine print into terms of service contracts.”

Specifically, Schiff told Meta that it should “provide explicit guarantees that external technical boundaries like paywalls and robots.txt protocols will be fully respected.”

RELATED ARTICLEMeta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical.Hanaa' TameezOctober 26, 2026“Meta’s verbal assurances that it will not supersede robots.txt files, which are voluntary server flags, do not appear to constitute enforceable legal protections,” Schiff wrote. “Without the insertion of specific language codifying Meta’s policy to respect robots.txt signals into the latest contractual terms, users lack any reliable means by which to protect their content.”

Schiff’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Schiff is the latest elected official in the United States to raise concerns about Meta’s commercial terms, which have now drawn bipartisan criticism. On Friday, Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee said that the terms “indicate Meta is attempting to exploit American creators and businesses by granting itself sweeping authority to scrape content from any website associated with Facebook and Instagram business accounts.”

The terms were previously set to take effect on October 30. Because the terms offered no way to opt out, news of them set off an outcry from news publishers, politicians, and press associations on both sides of the Atlantic. Meta then delayed the effective date of its new terms of service for business accounts to November 20.

On Tuesday, a coalition of Norwegian news publishers sued Meta over the terms and is asking the Oslo District Court to block the terms from going into effect. The legal action, led by the Norwegian Media Companies Association, is the first known lawsuit filed against Meta over its commercial terms.

“We are extending the effective date of our updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms to November 20 to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab in a statement Friday.

A Meta spokesperson said on October 17 that the company revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”

As of October 27, Meta has made no other changes to the terms aside from the implementation date. No version of the terms includes language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Scale a global AI content factory with approved local facts and human expertise to help AI search reflect each market's products, rules, and customers.

For more than 25 years, I have heard the same complaints from local marketing teams. “This doesn’t sound like us.” “Our customers don’t ask that question.” “That product isn’t even sold here.” “Why are we publishing a U.S. case study on the Japanese site?”

At headquarters, these complaints were usually treated as resistance. Local teams simply wanted control, and they didn’t understand the cost of supporting 30 or 40 markets. They were slowing down a process that had been carefully engineered for speed and consistency.

I understood that view. I also spent a lot of time explaining the local side of the argument to global teams who weren’t necessarily happy to hear it.

Now AI is giving enterprises the ability to produce content for every market faster and more cheaply than ever. And AI search is showing us, very clearly, what happens when that content is the same everywhere.

The local teams may have been right all along.

This article examines why the traditional global content model is breaking down in AI search, and how to build an AI-powered content factory that scales without erasing what makes each market unique.

Most multinational content operations were designed to solve one problem: how to publish the same message in many languages without the cost growing at the same rate as the number of markets.

The industry developed very good tools for that problem:

The key performance indicators followed the same logic: cost per word, TM leverage, reducing turnaround time, and accelerating time-to-market for a global launch. A high TM match rate was the key to maximizing KPIs and building confidence in uniform messaging.

When local teams pushed back, the rationale for pushback was hard to quantify. It was typically framed in terms of tone, nuance, or lack of cultural fit. When matched against a dashboard of cost savings, “it doesn’t feel local” rarely won the argument.

In traditional search, the cost of that decision was manageable. Hreflang told search engines which language and country version to show, so a translated page could still rank in its market. If the page was thin, it usually ranked a little lower. It didn’t disappear.

See also: Lost In Translation: How Language Changes Which Brand AI Recommends

AI search changes the unit of competition. Traditional search selected a page. AI search builds an answer from facts, passages, and evidence collected from many sources. That shift exposes a significant problem the traditional efficiency model created.

When search engines find a cluster of pages that are essentially the same, they don’t fully process and store every version. One version is selected as the canonical and processed in full. The others are treated more like alternate names that point back to it, carrying only enough information (URL, language, country) to be served in the right context.

AI systems refer to this as canonical tokenization, the process by which text across different languages is split, compressed, and processed. It is efficient for the search engine, and it works reasonably well when the job is to swap one URL for another on a results page.

It works much less well when an AI system is retrieving passages to build an answer. The passage it retrieves often comes from the canonical version, and once that passage is pulled out of the page, it no longer carries the URL that told everyone which market it belonged to.

I described the result in How AI’s Geo-Identification Failures Are Rewriting International SEO: When markets look the same, the strongest instance of your content wins. In most global companies, that is the U.S. or main English site.

So a buyer in Germany may get U.S. product availability. A patient in Japan may read about a product or use that is not approved there. A Spanish-language query from Spain may be answered with content written for Mexico.

This is the uncomfortable part for those of us who built global content programs. Translation memory was designed to maximize content reuse at scale. AI retrieval systems are designed to discard reuse.

Every sentence we reused across 30 markets now makes those markets look more alike to a machine. The higher our TM leverage, the stronger the case that our local pages were alternate versions of one global page, not unique sources worth retrieving in their own right.

When local teams said “this doesn’t feel like our market,” they were describing exactly what an AI system now concludes.

The twin engines of the marketing agility framework describe two forces every multinational has to run at the same time:

Research on the framework found that organizations perform best when both engines are running. Most global content programs, however, were built almost entirely around the global engine. The local engine was treated as a cost to be minimized, because local responsiveness was expensive. Every market-specific page needed a writer, a reviewer, and a budget line.

The usual way enterprises use AI today is to make the global engine faster: translate more content into more languages with fewer people. That produces more of the same near-identical pages, only quicker. It is a faster photocopier.

The bigger opportunity is to use AI to make the local engine more affordable. If AI handles the tedious and time-consuming activities of drafting, translation, structuring, and formatting, people in each market can spend their time on what only they can provide: local evidence, local questions, and local judgment.

A content factory built for AI search starts from a different premise. The product isn’t pages. The product is governed, market-scoped knowledge, and pages are one of the ways that knowledge is published.

Before anything is written or translated, the organization needs a single source of truth where its important claims live. Each fact should record:

This sounds like a governance exercise, and it is. It is also the only reliable way to prevent a fact that is true in one market from being published or retrieved as if it were true in all of them.

This is the most important change to the translation workflow. Not every sentence should be treated the same way.

Translation memory is still valuable for the first category. Product names, for example, should be identical across languages so that AI systems recognize them as the same entity. It is, however, a mistake to let TM leverage fill the second category. When a market-variable slot is empty, the factory should flag it, not copy the U.S. version into it.

With the fact registry and the segment rules in place, AI can now handle most of the production work by drafting from approved facts, translating and structuring pages around real questions, and verifying that the right source has been integrated for every market-variable slot.

This is where the cost savings come from now. The savings don’t come from reusing more sentences. They come from automating everything related to local evidence, so local teams can supply that evidence without bearing the full cost of producing the page.

The global engine contributes what should be identical everywhere; the local engine contributes what must differ. Both meet in the fact registry, and AI assembles each market’s pages from it.

“Keeping the human touch” is often understood as keeping a human post-editor at the end of the machine translation process. That role is becoming harder to defend on quality alone. A recent localization benchmark published here on Search Engine Journal found AI workflows outscored human translators in four of six content types.

I don’t read that as the end of human involvement. I read it as a signal that the human value has moved upstream.

In an AI content factory, people in each market are needed at four points:

Notice that these are the same things local teams were complaining about for years. They were never really asking for better translation. They were asking for their market’s reality to be represented.

This also changes how global SEO and content teams should be organized. The roles and service-level agreements I described in Effective SEO Organizational Structure For A Global Company need to include ownership of local evidence, not only local publishing.

Because AI systems retrieve passages that lose their URL context, each important passage has to carry its own market information. A few simple rules make a large difference:

These rules are easy to build into an AI-assisted workflow. They are much harder to apply consistently when 40 vendors are translating by hand.

Most global teams can tell you how many pages they published per market. Very few can tell you what an AI assistant says about them in each market.

That measurement should be part of the factory, not a one-time audit. Build a fixed set of priority prompts for each market, in the local language, and run them across the major AI assistants on a regular schedule. Then track four things:

Market leakage is the metric I’d watch most closely. It is the most direct measure of whether your local content is being recognized as local. It also gives local teams something they never had in the old model: evidence that their concerns are affecting the business.

Test in local languages, not just English. An English-only visibility check will not show you what a buyer in Seoul or Madrid is seeing.

Consider a composite example drawn from patterns common to global medical device manufacturers.

The company has a well-run global site with a dozen market versions. The technical setup, by traditional international SEO standards, is mostly correct, including hreflang and localized URLs. By traditional international SEO standards, it passes.

When viewed for geographical signals market by market, the picture is completely different:

None of these are translation problems. Each one is a missing piece of local knowledge, and each one was probably raised by someone in that market at some point.

The fix follows the factory model: Register the facts by market, mark which content is market-variable, have local teams supply the evidence and the questions, let AI assemble and structure the pages, and measure what AI assistants say in each language afterward.

The global content model wasn’t wrong to pursue efficiency. For a long time, local responsiveness at scale was simply too expensive, and search engines, using hreflang, were forgiving enough that translated pages could still compete.

AI search removes that forgiveness. When content is the same or very similar everywhere, AI systems collapse them into a single entity, and the strongest version speaks for every market.

AI also removes the excuse. The work that made local content expensive (drafting, translating, formatting, structuring) is exactly the work AI does well. What remains for people is the work local teams were asking to do all along.

So before you scale your content factory with AI, ask a simple question: Are you using AI to publish more of the same, faster? Or are you using it to give each market what it was asking for, finally?

#7345. Creators who show their sources build trust, survey finds

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Journalist-led research found audiences increased trust when news videos identified their sources, such as government documents and interviews.

RELATED ARTICLETwo-thirds of news influencers are men — and most have never worked for a news organizationSarah ScireNovember 18, 2024About one in five U.S. adults regularly gets their news from news creators on social media platforms, but it can be difficult for audiences to suss out which personalities to trust amid an avalanche of misinformation, hot takes, and polarizing content.

New research spearheaded by a team of journalists and political scientists shows that giving audiences a peek into the reporting process can help bolster their trust in the news.

Proof News, a nonprofit newsroom focused on tech accountability, in collaboration with researchers at the French university Sciences Po, shared social news videos with 2,000 U.S. adults to measure their perceptions of trustworthiness. Participants were randomly assigned one of Proof’s yet-to-be-published short-form news videos.

Some participants viewed videos with labels describing the sources, others saw videos with labels describing the newsroom’s ethical standards, and some saw videos without a label. The Sources labels appeared on cards embedded at the end of the video, like a credits reel, or were placed into the video description, the text accompanying the video.

Participants then rated the videos on various trust metrics. We found that labeling videos did increase trust — particularly a label that described the video sources in the description and, to a slightly lesser extent, a label describing newsroom standards in the credits.

This effect was particularly prominent among survey respondents who identified as Democrats or reported having high trust in science. Those groups, when shown the sourcing label in the description of a general news video, reported higher assessments of transparency and trust in the journalist.

There were fewer statistically significant increases in trust metrics with labels for text articles, but Sally Lehrman, founder of The Trust Project, said the findings were still intriguing.

“I’m excited to see the results,” Lehrman said. “Methods and references really do resonate…People are asking, where did the journalist get this information, and how can I trust it.”

As audiences increasingly turn to social media for news, there is a growing public discussion about how trustworthy creators are, especially when it comes to disclosing their funding and relationships. In January, The Wall Street Journal wrote about corporate and foreign interests using influencers to push agendas. In August, The Washington Post reported that the Pentagon secretly hired conservative military veterans with large online audiences to amplify Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s messaging, and a New York Times investigation revealed online influencers received funding from political campaigns without disclosing the connection in their videos.

Some creators have begun trying to distinguish themselves from this type of behavior through their own disclosure efforts.

RELATED ARTICLEWith Local News International, Dave Jorgenson becomes his own TikTok guyNeel DhaneshaSeptember 9, 2025Journalist and creator Dave Jorgenson, who has nearly 1 million followers across TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram, has started publishing a transparency report on his website, Local News International, revealing his sources of funding alongside his editorial standards.

Ultimately, he thinks disclosures of political funding should no longer be voluntary but mandatory. “Platforms should be regulating themselves,” Jorgenson said in an interview. “You can’t really force that unless there are laws.”

Proof used Jorgenson’s ethics and transparency statement as a model for the newsroom standards label in video testing and found that it increased viewers’ trust in the news outlet and the likelihood that they would share a general news story.

New York City is already considering disclosure requirements in the wake of revelations in the Columbia Journalism Review that exposed the inner workings of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s connections with influencers. The author of the article, Anya Schiffrin, a senior lecturer at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs, testified at a September city council meeting that creator relationships — both paid and unpaid — should be disclosed to viewers.

“It’s important for democracy that we have standards,” Schiffrin said.

RELATED ARTICLEProof News is Julia Angwin’s attempt to bring the scientific method to investigative journalismNeel DhaneshaMarch 21, 2024Proof News, which launched in 2024, pioneered an Ingredients label that takes cues from the scientific method and names the journalists’ hypothesis, sources, limitations, and the story’s findings.

To test whether the label worked to increase viewer trust for short-form vertical videos, we stripped down the Ingredients label to a bullet list of sources followed by an asterisk denoting the reporting limitations. The survey showed the label had a consistent positive effect when placed in the video description, the text box that is often located under the video.

The team also tested how labels performed on online text news articles. The survey showed 1,600 U.S. participants original, unpublished Proof News stories without a label, with a Proof Ingredients label, a label modeled after the Trust Project that described the reporting process, and a label describing newsroom standards.

There were fewer statistically significant increases in trust metrics with the print labels. The most significant findings were an increase in perception of transparency when the reporting process label was used on a polarizing story and an investigative story.

One possible explanation for the differing results between labeling video and text articles is the “ergonomics” of the medium, said Damien Bol, a professor at the Center for Political Research at Sciences Po who helped lead the survey design and data analysis.

“When reading a text, for example, people can quickly skim through it or skip parts of it, whereas a video forces them to follow the story second by second, even when watching at double speed,” Bol said. Different formats, Bol said, shape the “experience of consuming a news story.”

Earlier this month, Julia Angwin, an author of this article, hosted a private convening of creators at Harvard Kennedy School’s Shorenstein Center on Media, Politics and Public Policy to discuss creating shared standards that could be conveyed through a label or other public statement.

The group of 30 leading content creators from news, science communication, education, history, and other evidence-based fields discussed how they could distinguish their work by signaling to viewers their commitment to standards that could include disclosing funding sources and the use of artificial intelligence. Creator-led efforts to bring this to fruition are ongoing.

San Diego-based journalist Lisa Remillard, who has more than 4 million followers on her TikTok channel “The News Girl,” said that making videos with verified facts can feel like a small club. But if she can’t independently confirm something, she’s “not putting that out there.”

Remillard’s audience appears to appreciate transparency. Earlier this year, she published a video describing her editorial standards — and was richly rewarded for it. “I think clearly defining those ethics and standards resonated with my audience and gave them a reason to want to financially support my work,” Remillard said.

Jessica Yellin, the founder of the political podcast, YouTube channel, and social media brand “News Not Noise,” has also called for news creators to voluntarily sign a Creator Constitution, agreeing to journalistic standards such as citing sources, fixing errors, and disclosing financial relationships.

She said labeling sources is about the “signal.” Even if audiences don’t take the time to digest every word, Yellin observed, “It’s the act of showing it that matters.”

The way that data is produced is changing. For years it came from deterministic pipelines: many sources, weighted and decayed, one winner per attribute. Core Data is now moving to AI-native data management, where an agent pursues the evidence for an entity, decides every attribute over all of it, and records why. The company and contact agents already exist as working, measured prototypes. What does not exist yet is the machinery that runs them at production volume, proves every version before it ships, and lets researchers and product managers operate them without an engineer in the loop.

Vox users can watch videos and listen to podcasts in the app, but reading stories requires a paid subscription.

Vox has launched its first mobile application, the publication best known for its explanatory journalism announced Wednesday morning.

Growing membership is a “key priority,” managing editor for audience and membership Bill Carey said. Vox believes launching the app is one way to do that. A Vox membership costs $5 per month, or $60 per year, and offers ad-free versions of podcasts and unlimited access to all of the website’s contents.

RELATED ARTICLEVox is revamping its editorial strategy to redefine what ‘Voxxy’ meansHanaa' TameezNovember 8, 2021Strengthening its relationship to its audience is only becoming more important for Vox. The app launch comes at a time when news publishers are increasingly trying to keep users on their own platforms amid growing preferences for AI summaries, news creators, and industry-wide traffic declines.

“The move toward developing our membership program in the last couple of years has really been about understanding how important it is for us to build more community and to foster that loyalty [of our] audience,” Carey said. “When we were looking at that, it really felt like an app was a good way to continue pointing in that direction.”

Vox isn’t the only news outlet focusing on mobile apps. The Verge — Vox’s former sister publication under Vox Media — named traffic declines as one of the reasons why it plans to launch its own app next year. The Wall Street Journal’s head of digital, Taneth Evans, recently said that the Journal makes its app more useful to users by offering all of its mediums in one place. Evans also said that news publishers “need to give people reasons to open an app beyond simply offering news.”

“Websites will become a service for agents,” Evans said. “Apps are gonna be the thing that humans will connect with.”

Vox declined to provide website traffic numbers, but data from Comscore shows that the website’s unique visitors decreased by 36% year-over-year between September 2025 (7.4 million) and September 2026 (4.8 million). Archived data from SimilarWeb shows the site had 20.8 million visits in September 2021.

“Vox isn’t immune to the larger trends that have led to web traffic declines in recent years, but those only represent a portion of our audience,” Carey said in an email. “Vox is focused on building audience engagement across platforms, with social video views up 86% year-over-year and newsletter audience up 14%.”

“Even if there wasn’t a decline in search traffic, as everyone has been seeing — and we still get members from search — we want to create that relationship with our audience,” publisher and editor-in-chief Swati Sharma said. “People know Vox and they have a relationship with Vox. We have a younger audience that’s on all of these different platforms. I think it is definitely a part of building that relationship ourselves.”

That the app makes all Vox content accessible in one place for current and future members also signals the “un-siloing” of the newsroom overall, Sharma said. Vox currently has 78 editorial employees.

RELATED ARTICLESwati Sharma is leading a new era in Vox’s mission to “explain the world”Hanaa' TameezMay 6, 2021When Sharma, who has helmed Vox.com since 2021, first arrived, she found that Vox’s main mediums (text, audio, and video) “weren’t in service of one another.” The “silos” allowed teams to build their own audiences and products. But while teams discussed story ideas with each other and during editorial meetings, “they all [needed] to go into their creative spaces and find what works for their medium and not be in service of just one larger section.”

That’s changed over the past five years, Sharma said. Each team — text, video, and audio — does a little bit of everything now. Text reporters appear on podcasts and in videos, while podcasters and hosts also write their own newsletters.

“In a lot of newsrooms, there’s one dominant form, and at Vox, there wasn’t. They’re all really important,” Sharma said. “[Senior correspondent] Dylan Scott is on our Unexplainable podcast talking about Alzheimer’s. [Host and editorial director] Astead Herndon does a newsletter and a Substack Live every week, and he does a podcast. That’s the future for us, and that’s where our whole newsroom is moving, where those silos are done and you can basically do everything.”

#7338. 5,900 Google Ads Accounts Show Ad Strength Wins Impressions – Not Conversions via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Brad Geddes analyzed 5,900+ Google Ads accounts. Higher ad strength RSAs win more impressions, but pinned, lower-rated ads often convert better. What to change.

If you run responsive search ads, Google is now steering more impressions toward whichever ad in an ad group carries the higher ad strength rating. That ad has the better conversion rate only 45% of the time.

A new study by Brad Geddes, co-founder of Adalysis, analyzed more than 5,900 Google Ads accounts to answer a question PPC managers have argued about since RSAs became the default ad format. Does higher ad strength lead to better performance?

His answer is yes for some ads and no for others. The difference comes down to one setting, which is pinning.

I’ve known Brad since May 2011, when he became the PPC Faculty Chair at Market Motive while I was the faculty chair of Video and Content Marketing. And as one of the co-authors of Digital Marketing Fundamentals, which Wiley published in 2023, I asked Brad to contribute the chapter on Digital Advertising. So, I can vouch for his Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness (E-E-A-T) in PPC and paid media.

When Brad previewed the findings in a LinkedIn post last week, calling ad strength “one of Google Ads’ most misunderstood metrics,” I went back to read his full study, which follows up on the company’s 2022 ad strength study. That gives us a four-year view of how Google’s ad serving has drifted.

Here is what the data shows, where it collides with what Google says, and what I’d change in your accounts before holiday traffic peaks.

Start with the official position, because Brad’s numbers only become interesting against it.

Google’s Help Center describes ad strength as a guide for the ad creation stage. It says the rating “doesn’t directly influence your ad’s serving eligibility” and isn’t used to calculate Ad Rank, Quality Score, or auction wins.

Ginny Marvin, Google’s Ads Product Liaison, has been just as direct. In a March 2024 post on X, she wrote that ad strength “isn’t used directly in the auction & shouldn’t limit your testing.”

I take Google at its word on the mechanics. But “not an auction input” and “doesn’t affect which of your ads gets shown” are two different claims, and Brad’s data speaks to the second one.

The most useful part of Brad’s study isolates ad groups with two active RSAs that carry different ad strength ratings. Both ads share the same keywords, bids, and budget, which strips out a lot of noise.

In those ad groups, the higher-rated ad received more impressions 63% of the time. An Excellent ad beat a Poor ad on impressions in 78% of ad groups. Ads two ratings apart, such as Excellent versus Average or Good versus Poor, won 66% of the time. Even the closest matchup, Good versus Average, went to the higher-rated ad 59% of the time.

The higher-rated ad had the higher CTR in 52.5% of ad groups, barely better than a coin flip. It had the higher conversion rate in only 45%, which means the lower-rated ad converted better in 55% of ad groups. On conversions per 1,000 impressions, a metric Adalysis calls CPI, the lower-rated ad won 54.3% of the time.

Then there’s cost. The lower-rated ad had the lower CPA in 51.5% of ad groups, and across all ad groups the higher-rated ads ran an 11.8% higher CPA. In Brad’s example, a lower-rated ad with a $100 CPA would face a higher-rated rival at $111.80.

Brad’s warning for anyone running ad tests is Google “will serve the higher-rated ad more often, even if it has a worse conversion rate or CPI.”

See also: Why a Sky-High CTR Does Not Mean Your Ads Are Actually Working

Because Adalysis ran a similar study in 2022, Brad can show which way Google’s serving has moved.

Google is leaning harder on the higher-rated ad when it picks which ad to show, and that pick lines up with clicks a little better than it did four years ago. It does not line up with conversions any better. Brad concludes that Google “has increased its reliance on ad strength to determine what ad to show in an auction over the years.”

That’s his reading of observational data, and Google would likely dispute the word “reliance.”

Before anyone decides ad strength is useless, look at who the lower-rated ads are.

Brad attributes most of their conversion edge to pinning. In most of the mixed-strength ad groups, one ad was pinned and the other wasn’t. Pinned ads tend to earn lower ratings, and they also tend to post higher conversion rates.

That makes sense to anyone who has pinned a headline on purpose. You pin a price, a required disclaimer, or a qualifier because you want to filter the click rather than chase it. Ad strength rewards variety and keyword coverage, and a pinned ad written to pre-qualify buyers works against both.

The unpinned results look very different. Among unpinned ads, CTR rose with every step up in ad strength, and so did CPI. Conversion rates rose slightly at each step except Poor to Average. For those ads, Brad’s conclusion is that chasing a higher rating generally pays off.

So, the honest summary isn’t that ad strength doesn’t matter. It’s that ad strength predicts performance well when you leave Google’s system alone and poorly when you’ve deliberately overridden it.

See also: Google Ads Bid Strategy Testing: What Changed In 2026

Only a third of unpinned ads in the dataset reached Excellent, and Brad’s asset counts show why stuffing in headlines won’t get you there.

Without pinning, an ad can reach Good with as few as seven assets. For Excellent, Brad recommends at least 11 different headlines. Volume alone doesn’t do it, though. Only 44% of ads with 15 or more headlines reached Excellent, and in the most extreme case, an ad with 38 assets was still rated Poor.

Once you pin, the minimum asset count to reach Good jumps to 10. Pinning two positions now caps an ad at Good and often leaves it at Poor or Average, which is stricter than what Adalysis saw in 2022. If you pin all three headline positions, Brad suggests aiming for about 13 assets.

There is a workaround. Pinning three or more different assets to the same position still leaves room for Excellent, while pinning only one or two caps the ad at Good. Position matters too, since headline one carries more weight than headline two, which carries more than headline three.

I’ve been in paid search since 2003, and Google has asked advertisers to trust a diagnostic label for most of that time. Quality Score came first. Google’s Ads Product Liaison has said it is also a diagnostic rather than an auction input, yet the expected CTR, ad relevance, and landing page signals behind it clearly shape what we pay. Ad strength looks like the same kind of label.

My read is that Google and Brad can both be right. The rating itself may never enter the auction. But the things that raise it, more distinct headlines, better keyword coverage, and fewer pins, give Google’s system more combinations to work with when it predicts which of your ads will earn the click. In your account, the outcome is the same either way. The higher-rated ad gets the traffic.

That’s where I think practitioners should push back. Google’s ad selection appears tuned to clicks, and your business generally gets paid on conversions. An 11.8% CPA gap across ad groups is not a rounding error at holiday budgets. Treat ad strength as a traffic allocator you have to manage, and stop treating it as a score you have to win.

See also: How To Measure PPC Performance When AI Controls The Auction

Sort your RSAs by pinning status before you read a single rating. Tag each ad as unpinned, partly pinned, or fully pinned in Google Ads Editor or a report export. The rating means something different in each group, so judge each group on its own.

Push unpinned ads to Excellent with variety, not volume. Brad recommends at least 11 headlines that mix keywords, benefits, features, calls to action, and authority statements. If an unpinned ad sits at Average with 15 headlines, the likely culprit is repetition. Rewrite the near-duplicates before you add more.

Rebuild pinned ads instead of abandoning them. Brad’s process is to remove the pins, build the ad to Excellent, then re-pin and keep adding assets until the rating reaches at least Average, or Good if you pin a single headline. Where you must pin, pin three or more variations to that position. If you pin all three headlines, plan on about 13 assets.

Judge tests on CPI and CPA, and give mismatched tests more time. Brad says it’s fine to run ads with different ratings in the same ad group. Expect the lower-rated ad to collect far fewer impressions, though, since an Excellent ad took the impression lead in nearly four of five matchups against a poor one. That stretches the time it takes to reach statistical significance. If the lower-rated, pinned ad wins on CPA, keep it running. Don’t pause a winner to fix a label.

Brad closes his study with a line every PPC manager should keep handy. He writes that “often, the human ability to create compelling ads will outperform the machine’s ability to serve the ads properly.”

I agree with one caveat. The machine still decides how often your best human-written ad gets seen. So, ad strength is something to check against your own conversion data, ad group by ad group, rather than a grade to celebrate.

Google tells us what the rating isn’t. Brad’s 5,900 accounts tell us what it does.

Meta will complete “a full consultation” with news industry leaders before implementing its controversial new terms — even if it means another delay, an executive for the social media company announced today.

“We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms. Until then our existing terms remain in place.”

Meta did not answer Nieman Lab’s questions about which news industry groups and leaders Meta plans to consult.

The proposed terms have drawn criticism because they would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and potentially allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models, with no option to opt out. Last week, Meta announced it would push back implementation of its new terms to November 20 in order to “explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab. Meta had previously revised its new terms to remove the word “train.” No version of the terms has included language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

Shortly after Stone’s announcement, a Norwegian court blocked Meta’s terms from taking effect on November 20 until the court had assessed their legality, the country’s public broadcaster NRK reported.

“We are satisfied that the court has agreed with us that Meta holds a dominant position in the relevant market and that the new terms are unreasonable,” said Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, MBL’s board chair, in a news release. “We are also pleased that the court recognizes that the alternative is that media companies risk losing control over editorial content built up over many years.”

Since Nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15, publishers and politicians around the world have pushed back, filing complaints with national competition authorities, calling on the European Commission to investigate, and writing letters to Meta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Two United States senators — California Democrat Adam Schiff and Tennessee Republican Marsha Blackburn — each separately wrote to Zuckerberg, insisting that the company withdraw the terms as they’re currently written.

“After I raised serious concerns about Meta’s plans to scrape and abuse creators’ content, I am pleased the company is finally acknowledging the concerns of publishers and content creators,” Blackburn said in a statement to Nieman Lab on Wednesday. “While this is a step in the right direction, a vague promise to consult with industry stakeholders and potentially delay implementation is not nearly enough. Meta must commit to meaningful changes that protect the intellectual property rights of American creators, and I will continue holding the company accountable until it does.”

On October 21, the European Publishers Council signed onto a joint letter to the European Commission, asking the Commission to block the terms from taking effect. The letter claims that Meta’s terms violate the Digital Markets Act, a law passed in 2020 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region.

EPC executive director Angela Mills Wade said on Wednesday that the organization has not heard from Meta about its letter or its concerns.

“We welcome Meta’s offer to consult publishers fully, and to delay implementation if necessary,” Mills Wade said in an email to Nieman Lab. “However, that consultation must lead to binding contractual safeguards…Using Meta’s services to reach audiences or advertise should not mean granting wider rights to exploit publishers’ journalism, whether collected from websites or uploaded to its platforms. Publishers must retain control over additional uses of their content, including for AI, and the ability to negotiate licenses and payment.”

This story has been updated to include a statement from Marsha Blackburn.

#7334. Rank Trackers Find Google Results About One Word Of A Query via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Two rank trackers' data shows unrelated Google results that follow one word of the query, mostly below the top spots. Here's how to check a ranking drop.

In mid-September, most unrelated results discovered by SE Ranking using Google rank checking were only about one word of the original search term. Almost all of them started at position 9 or worse.

SE Ranking released an analysis today based on 10,000 Google US desktop keywords it tracks for research purposes. Rank tracking firm Nozzle documented a related pattern in an Oct. 22 report on what it describes as Google ignoring part of a query. According to Nozzle’s findings, page 2 started dropping words on Sept. 16 while page 1 dropped words four days later (Sept. 20). Both firms sell rank tracking software and track ranks through their respective products.

On Oct. 23 I covered how rank tracking providers say they handle the altered Google results; prior to that, on Oct. 14 Roger Montti reported Nozzle’s initial analysis. Both data sets show that most changes occurred in positions below the top positions. Nozzle’s data shows that most of the changes it saw occur on page 2. As such, when reviewing your late September/October ranking reports, check drops below the top positions and on page 2 first.

The primary example of a single-word result set offered by SE Ranking is for the search term “business bank line of credit.” The top 9 results on this search were all financial institutions (banks/lenders) such as Chase Bank, PNC Bank and LendingTree. Results found on page 2 were unrelated to banking or lending as they included videos of music, the LINE messaging application and The Line Hotel; therefore these results only used the word “line” in relation to the original query, rather than answering the query.

In 84% of the cases SE Ranking flagged, the unrelated listings were about one word of the query. The rest followed two or more words. Single-word keywords in its data never came back with unrelated results, which the company says could be because there was no other word for the results to follow.

In one of Nozzle’s examples, “easy strawberry jam” on Sept. 30, the AI Overview still gave a jam recipe while the organic results were about the word “easy,” including the TV series Easy. Nozzle found the page title still showed the full query on 99.8% of the pages that dropped words, with no “Showing results for” notice.

SE Ranking saved up to 50 organic results per keyword, and none of the groups of unrelated results it found started in the top five. They started at positions 6 to 8 in 3.5% of affected result sets and at position 9 or lower in the other 96.5%. SE Ranking notes that a quick look at the top results could make such a page seem fine.

Since Sept. 16, page 2 ignored part of the query on 12.6% of the desktop searches Nozzle could judge on both pages, compared with 2.2% for page 1. On 93.6% of the page 2s that dropped words, page 1 still answered the query.

The way SE Ranking and Nozzle assess a search issue differs, therefore their rates cannot be compared directly to one another.

On Sept. 16, the estimated percentage of keywords in SE Ranking’s sample whose saved result list included any unrelated listing was 0.09%. On Sept. 17 the estimate was 57.3%, and by Sept. 24, which was the end of the test period, the percentage had grown to 67.2%.

Nozzle will flag a search results page if a term that has historically appeared in search results for the keyword appears in 20% or less of those results. Using this method, Nozzle measured that page 1 or page 2 lost terms on approximately 13.9% of the desktop searches it judged on both pages from Sept. 16 through Oct. 21. The highest rate of losing terms was approximately 39.9% on Sept. 28. Nozzle also observed short-term spikes in the occurrence of the pattern since March.

Nozzle viewed this as a different failure type from the “poisoned” search results it reported in October where the query is still answered; however the keyword’s typical websites do not appear. According to Nozzle’s data, when a page lost terms, the keyword’s subsequent search page(s) within 3 days provided an answer to the query about 85.8% of the time.

The numbers shown in SE Ranking’s daily report spanned from Sept. 17 through Sept. 24. SE Ranking’s baseline tests run in October utilized differing collection settings. A sampling of cases was assessed by two independent AI reviewers, and 40 disputed cases were manually reviewed. SE Ranking adds that its data only covers organic listings and can’t tell Google’s intent or what searchers saw, and that Google hasn’t publicly explained the results.

SE Ranking notes that if an unrelated result has taken over the lower part of a search engine results page (SERP), a website which normally appears there may appear to be missing from a tracker report without its rank necessarily changing for people using the Google search engine.

Before reporting a late September/October drop at position 9 or lower or on a second page, go through the collected results from your last update to see if the pages that took your place were related to just one word in the query. Then go back to your next update and look at Search Console data for impressions and clicks on the same query, as SE Ranking suggests.

AccuRanker, whose page 1 history check I described on Oct. 23, has updated its post to say pages 2 and beyond have a related problem, with results for only one word of the query. It says it will cover that in a separate article. Check with your tracker to see whether it reviews page 2 or stops at page 1.
